stem: Hundreds of Linux instances in three AZs must share a POSIX file system for content that is read often but rarely changed, at the lowest cost. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: Amazon S3 mounted as a file system on every instance
Amazon EBS Multi-Attach io2 volumes shared by all instances
FSx for Windows File Server with SMB shares
Amazon EFS with lifecycle to Infrequent Access

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EFS is a regional, multi-AZ POSIX file system mountable by many Linux clients. Lifecycle management moves colder files to the lower-cost Infrequent Access class.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EBS Multi-Attach: limited to a few instances in one AZ and needs a cluster-aware file system.
• S3 as a file system: not POSIX-compliant; mount tools have semantic limitations.
• FSx for Windows: SMB for Windows workloads, not the natural fit for Linux POSIX sharing.

Key takeaway: shared POSIX files across AZs → EFS; cost → lifecycle to IA.

stem: A distributed application spans API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB, and the team needs to trace individual requests end-to-end to identify which component is causing intermittent latency. Which service should they use?

choices.text: AWS X-Ray
AWS Config
Amazon Inspector
Amazon CloudWatch Logs alone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
X-Ray traces requests across API Gateway, Lambda, and DynamoDB to show where time is spent.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: configuration.
• Inspector: vulnerabilities.
• Logs alone: no end-to-end request view.

Key takeaway: end-to-end request tracing → X-Ray.

stem: An application uploads large video files (5 to 20 GB each) from users distributed globally directly to an S3 bucket in us-east-1. Users in Asia and Australia report slow, inconsistent upload speeds. Which combination of S3 features should the architect implement to improve upload performance without changing the bucket's Region?

choices.text: Switch to the S3 One Zone-IA storage class
Enable S3 Versioning and Cross-Region Replication
Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration and use multipart upload
Increase the size of the EC2 instance hosting the upload application

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transfer Acceleration speeds long-distance uploads via edge locations, and multipart upload parallelizes and retries parts of large files.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One Zone-IA: storage class.
• Versioning and CRR: after upload.
• Bigger EC2: users upload directly.

Key takeaway: large global uploads → acceleration + multipart.

stem: A team wants an email when forecast monthly spend will exceed $10,000, and also wants a Slack alert when actual spend passes 80% of that budget. Which service fits BEST?

choices.text: AWS Cost and Usage Report delivered to S3
AWS Budgets forecast and actual alerts
AWS Cost Explorer saved reports
Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Budgets supports thresholds on forecast and actual spend and notifies through email or SNS, which can feed Slack via AWS Chatbot.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Cost Explorer: analysis, not proactive alerts.
• CUR: detailed billing data files; no alerting.
• Trusted Advisor: optimization tips; no budget alerts.

Key takeaway: thresholds and alerts on spend → Budgets.

stem: During a Lambda deployment managed by AWS CodeDeploy, an associated CloudWatch alarm monitoring function error rate enters ALARM state partway through the traffic shift. What does CodeDeploy do if automatic rollback is enabled for that alarm?

choices.text: CodeDeploy ignores the alarm and continues shifting traffic to completion
CodeDeploy pauses indefinitely until the stack is deleted manually
CodeDeploy immediately deletes the Lambda function entirely
It stops and rolls traffic back to the prior version

explanation:
Why this is correct:
When an associated alarm fires, CodeDeploy stops the deployment and rolls traffic back to the previous version (if configured).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ignores alarm: no.
• Pauses indefinitely: no.
• Deletes the function: no.

Key takeaway: alarms trigger automatic rollback.

stem: A team is choosing between a canary deployment configuration, where a small initial percentage of traffic is held for a wait period and then the rest shifts all at once, and a linear deployment configuration, where traffic increases in small, equal increments over multiple steps, for a Lambda function update. What is the key tradeoff between the two?

choices.text: Linear can't use automatic rollback, but canary always can
Canary: one small step then all; linear: gradual steps, slower but safer
Canary deployments are available only for EC2, not for Lambda
Canary and linear always take the same total time to complete

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Canary shifts a small portion once, then the rest. Linear shifts in equal steps over time, which is slower but more gradual.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Linear can't roll back: it can.
• Canary EC2-only: available for Lambda and ECS.
• Same total time: differs.

Key takeaway: canary = two steps; linear = many steps.

stem: A request intermittently takes 8 seconds. Metrics show the latency spike, logs show a timeout message, but the team can't tell which of 6 services caused it. Which signal should they use next?

choices.text: CloudTrail data events enabled for each service in the request path
More CloudWatch metrics at 1-second resolution
X-Ray traces showing time spent per service segment
Longer log retention on all log groups

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Metrics show that something is wrong and logs show events, but traces show where time went across services for a single request.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More metrics: still aggregates, not per request.
• Longer retention: doesn't locate the slow hop.
• CloudTrail: AWS API calls, not the request path.

Key takeaway: metrics = what, logs = detail, traces = where.

stem: A team wants to define infrastructure in TypeScript with loops, shared libraries, and unit tests, while still deploying through CloudFormation. Which tool fits?

choices.text: AWS Service Catalog
AWS Config rules
AWS CDK
AWS OpsWorks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The AWS CDK uses general-purpose languages (TypeScript, Python, and others) to define infrastructure, supports reusable constructs and unit tests, and synthesizes CloudFormation templates for deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Service Catalog: distributes approved products; not an authoring language.
• OpsWorks: Chef or Puppet configuration management.
• Config rules: compliance checks.

Key takeaway: code-first IaC on CloudFormation → CDK.

stem: A 3 TB tabular training set in S3 is read by Athena for feature exploration (a few columns at a time) and by SageMaker training. Scans are slow and costly with CSV. Which format and layout fit BEST?

choices.text: One large Avro file so readers always get the full schema
JSON Lines with Snappy compression per record
Gzipped CSV, split into 1 GB files for parallel reads
Parquet, partitioned by a common filter column

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Parquet is columnar: queries read only the needed columns and skip row groups using statistics. Partitioning by a frequent filter (for example, date) prunes data further, and SageMaker and Athena both read Parquet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Gzipped CSV: still reads every column, and gzip files aren't splittable.
• JSON Lines: row-based and verbose.
• One Avro file: row-based, and a single file limits parallelism.

Key takeaway: analytics-style reads → columnar + partitioned.

stem: A data engineering team currently stores ML training data as Apache ORC files that were originally created by an on-premises Hive cluster. They want to migrate the pipeline to use Parquet instead. Which statement correctly compares the two formats in the context of AWS analytics and ML services?

choices.text: Both are columnar with compression and pushdown; Parquet has broader AWS support
ORC and Parquet are both row-based formats, so switching gives no functional benefit
ORC files can be read only by Hadoop and are incompatible with every AWS service
Parquet can't store nested or complex data types, while ORC can

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ORC and Parquet are both columnar formats with compression and predicate pushdown. Parquet has broader support across AWS analytics and ML tools, so switching mainly improves compatibility.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Row-based: both are columnar.
• ORC Hadoop-only: widely readable.
• Parquet can't store nested types: it can.

Key takeaway: columnar formats speed analytics; Parquet is the most widely supported.

stem: An ML engineer is preparing image classification training data to use with a SageMaker built-in algorithm that expects the Apache MXNet RecordIO format for maximum I/O throughput during training. Which format should be used to package the images and labels together for this purpose?

choices.text: Pipe input mode with a CSV manifest file only
Parquet files partitioned by class label
RecordIO packing images and labels (im2rec)
RecordIO-protobuf bundling images as JSON arrays

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The built-in image classification algorithm efficiently reads RecordIO files that pack images and labels (created with im2rec).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pipe mode with CSV manifest only: not the format.
• Parquet by label: not supported for images.
• RecordIO-protobuf with JSON arrays: wrong packing.

Key takeaway: image classification input → RecordIO (im2rec).

stem: A streaming ingestion job writes semi-structured event data with an evolving schema (new optional fields added over time) to a data lake used for feature engineering. Downstream Spark jobs frequently break when new fields appear. Which data format provides built-in schema evolution support along with compact binary serialization to address this issue?

choices.text: Avro, which embeds a schema and supports evolution
CSV, because it is simple to parse and widely supported
Plain text logs, because they require no schema at all
BMP images, because they are a compact binary format

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Avro embeds its schema and supports schema evolution, such as adding optional fields.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CSV: no schema.
• Plain text: no structure.
• BMP: images.

Key takeaway: evolving schemas → Avro.

stem: A team runs distributed training jobs on Amazon SageMaker that require a shared POSIX-compliant file system mounted concurrently by multiple training instances, with sub-millisecond latency and existing NetApp-based snapshot and cloning workflows carried over from an on-premises NetApp environment. Which storage option best fits these requirements?

choices.text: Amazon S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval
Amazon S3 Standard
Amazon FSx for NetApp ONTAP
Amazon EFS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
FSx for NetApp ONTAP provides a shared, low-latency POSIX file system with native NetApp snapshots and cloning, preserving existing workflows.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glacier IR and S3: object storage, not POSIX.
• EFS: POSIX but no ONTAP snapshot/clone features.

Key takeaway: keep NetApp workflows → FSx for ONTAP.

stem: Data scientists, Athena, EMR, and SageMaker all need the same raw and curated datasets, with lifecycle to cheaper tiers and fine-grained table permissions. Which foundation fits?

choices.text: S3 data lake with Glue Catalog and Lake Formation
EFS as the primary store, with a copy per team in each account
One large EBS volume shared by all processing instances
An RDS database that stores every dataset as tables

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 is durable, low cost, and readable by all these services; the Glue Data Catalog provides shared schemas, Lake Formation manages table and column permissions, and lifecycle policies tier data by age.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shared EBS: single-AZ and attaches to few instances.
• RDS: not built for petabyte raw files or ML training input.
• EFS copies: more expensive and duplicated.

Key takeaway: ML data lake = S3 + catalog + governance.

stem: A fraud detection ML pipeline needs to ingest continuous clickstream events in real time, retain them for replay by multiple consumer applications, and later use them to build near-real-time features. Which AWS service is designed for this kind of durable, replayable streaming ingestion?

choices.text: Amazon SQS Standard queue
AWS Glue crawler
Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Kinesis Data Streams ingests continuous events in real time, retains them for replay, and supports multiple consumers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SQS: no replay for multiple consumers.
• Glue crawler: cataloging.
• Transfer Acceleration: uploads.

Key takeaway: real-time replayable streams → Kinesis.

stem: An organization already operates a self-managed Apache Kafka cluster on-premises for streaming ingestion and wants to move this workload to AWS with minimal operational overhead for cluster management while retaining the Kafka API. Which AWS service should they choose over building a new solution on Kinesis Data Streams?

choices.text: Amazon Redshift Streaming Ingestion
Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose only
AWS Glue Data Catalog
Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amazon MSK runs Apache Kafka as a managed service, letting existing Kafka producers and consumers move with minimal change.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redshift streaming: a consumer, not Kafka.
• Firehose only: not Kafka-compatible.
• Glue Catalog: metadata.

Key takeaway: existing Kafka → MSK.

stem: A team needs to compute rolling window aggregations (such as a 5-minute moving average) directly on a Kinesis Data Stream to generate real-time features for a fraud-scoring model, with exactly-once processing semantics. Which AWS-managed processing framework is purpose-built for this kind of stateful stream processing?

choices.text: AWS Glue DataBrew
Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink
Amazon Athena
AWS Batch

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Managed Service for Apache Flink computes rolling window aggregations on streams in real time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DataBrew: batch prep.
• Athena: queries data at rest.
• Batch: batch jobs.

Key takeaway: streaming windows → Flink.
services: Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink

stem: An ML team wants to continuously deliver streaming IoT sensor data into Amazon S3 in Parquet format, automatically batching and converting records without managing custom consumer code, so a Glue ETL job can later transform it for training. Which service should they use for this delivery step?

choices.text: AWS DataSync scheduled transfers
Amazon SNS topic subscriptions
Firehose with format conversion
Kinesis Data Streams alone

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Firehose delivers streaming data to S3 and can convert records to Parquet using a Glue schema.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DataSync: file transfers.
• SNS: notifications.
• Kinesis Data Streams alone: no S3 delivery or conversion.

Key takeaway: stream to S3 in Parquet → Firehose format conversion.

stem: A self-managed training instance running on Amazon EC2 needs consistently high, predictable IOPS to read large shuffled batches from a local block volume during training, and default gp3 baseline performance is insufficient. Which EBS volume type should be attached to guarantee a specified high IOPS level?

choices.text: EBS Throughput Optimized HDD (st1)
EBS Provisioned IOPS SSD (io1/io2)
EBS General Purpose SSD (gp2) only
EBS Cold HDD (sc1)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Provisioned IOPS SSD (io1/io2) delivers consistently high, predictable IOPS.

Why the other options are wrong:
• st1 and sc1: HDD for throughput or cold data.
• gp2 only: burst-based, less predictable.

Key takeaway: predictable IOPS → io1/io2.

stem: A data scientist wants to join S3 and Redshift data visually, apply 20 common transforms, see a quick-model feature importance, and then export the flow to a SageMaker pipeline without writing Spark. Which tool fits?

choices.text: AWS Glue Studio with custom PySpark scripts
SageMaker Ground Truth with custom labeling jobs
SageMaker Data Wrangler
Amazon Athena with a set of saved SQL queries

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data Wrangler imports from sources such as S3 and Redshift, offers built-in transforms, data insights and quick-model analysis, and exports flows to processing jobs or SageMaker Pipelines.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue Studio scripts: requires writing Spark.
• Athena queries: SQL only, no quick model or pipeline export.
• Ground Truth: labeling, not data prep.

Key takeaway: visual ML data prep → Data Wrangler.

stem: A company trains multiple models that need to reuse the same engineered customer features, and also needs a low-latency store to serve those same feature values consistently to real-time inference endpoints. Which SageMaker capability addresses both the training-time and inference-time feature consistency requirement?

choices.text: SageMaker Clarify
SageMaker Model Registry
SageMaker Data Wrangler
SageMaker Feature Store

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Feature Store stores engineered features for reuse across models, with online and offline stores.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Clarify: bias and explainability.
• Model Registry: models.
• Data Wrangler: preparation.

Key takeaway: shared features → Feature Store.

stem: Within SageMaker Feature Store, a team notices that features written to the online store are available almost immediately for real-time inference, while the same features take longer to become queryable in bulk for model training. Which explanation correctly describes this behavior?

choices.text: Online is low-latency; offline (S3) updates asynchronously with lag
There's no difference; both stores update at exactly the same time by design
The online store is S3-backed and the offline store is an in-memory cache
The offline store supports only writes and cannot be queried at all

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The online store serves low-latency lookups immediately. The offline store in S3 is updated asynchronously for training and history.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same timing: no.
• Swapped storage: incorrect.
• Offline can't be queried: it can (Athena).

Key takeaway: online = real-time; offline = historical in S3.

stem: A team is training a SageMaker built-in Linear Learner model on a very large tabular dataset and wants to minimize training time by using Pipe mode to stream data directly from S3 instead of downloading the full dataset to local disk (File mode). Which trade-off should the team consider when choosing Pipe mode with RecordIO-protobuf formatted data?

choices.text: Pipe mode requires the whole dataset to fit in instance memory, unlike File mode
Pipe mode works only with CSV files and cannot use RecordIO-protobuf
Pipe streams data (faster start, less disk) but limits access patterns like full shuffles
File mode is always faster than Pipe mode regardless of dataset size

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Pipe mode streams data from S3, speeding job start and reducing disk needs, but data is read sequentially rather than randomly accessed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Must fit in memory: no.
• CSV only: supports RecordIO-protobuf.
• File always faster: not for large data.

Key takeaway: large datasets → Pipe (or FastFile) mode.

stem: A processing step must pass a small set of hyperparameters and schema metadata to a training step, readable by humans and by standard libraries, and diff-friendly in Git. Which format fits?

choices.text: JSON
A pickled Python object
RecordIO-protobuf
Parquet

explanation:
Why this is correct:
JSON is human-readable, supported everywhere, and produces clear diffs, which suits small configuration and metadata files.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Parquet: built for large tabular data, not small configs.
• RecordIO-protobuf: binary training data format.
• Pickle: Python-only, not human-readable, and unsafe to load from untrusted sources.

Key takeaway: small config → JSON; bulk data → columnar/binary formats.

stem: An ML engineering team is deciding between batch ingestion (periodic S3 uploads processed by Glue ETL jobs) and streaming ingestion (Kinesis Data Streams with continuous consumers) for a recommendation model's feature pipeline. The business requires features to reflect user activity within seconds, not hours. Which ingestion approach and trade-off applies?

choices.text: Neither approach can achieve sub-minute feature freshness on AWS
Streaming with Kinesis: fresher features, more ops and compute cost
Batch, because Glue ETL jobs can run every second at no extra cost
Batch, because it is always cheaper and equally timely

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Streaming with Kinesis gives fresher features at the cost of more operations and continuous compute.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Neither achieves sub-minute: streaming does.
• Glue every second free: no.
• Batch equally timely: no.

Key takeaway: freshness costs operational complexity.

stem: A numeric feature has 15% missing values, missing at random, with a skewed distribution and outliers. The model must not see information from the validation set. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Median imputation fit on training data only
Drop all rows that contain any missing value
Mean imputation computed on the full dataset
Replace missing values with zero everywhere

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The median is robust to skew and outliers, and fitting the imputer on the training split only (then applying it to validation and test) avoids leakage. Adding a missing-indicator feature can also help.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Full-dataset mean: leaks validation information and is skewed by outliers.
• Dropping rows: loses 15% of data or more.
• Zero: distorts the distribution unless zero is meaningful.

Key takeaway: impute robustly and fit preprocessing only on training data.

stem: Sensor readings include rare extreme values: some are hardware glitches, others are real failure events the model must learn. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Flag outliers, keep real events, fix glitches
Remove every point beyond three standard deviations
One-hot encode the numeric sensor values
Min-max scale the data so outliers disappear

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Outliers aren't automatically errors. Investigate them with domain knowledge and rules: remove or correct glitches, keep genuine rare events, and consider robust scaling or clipping.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Blind removal: deletes the failures the model must learn.
• Min-max scaling: doesn't remove outliers; they compress other values.
• One-hot numeric: inappropriate.

Key takeaway: outlier handling requires judgment, not a blanket rule.

stem: A raw customer dataset ingested from multiple source systems contains duplicate records with slightly different formatting (e.g., inconsistent capitalization in email addresses) that must be cleaned before feature engineering. Which AWS service provides a visual, no-code interface with built-in transformations to detect and remove such duplicates and standardize text formatting?

choices.text: Amazon Redshift Spectrum
AWS Glue DataBrew
Amazon Kinesis Data Analytics
AWS Lambda only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue DataBrew provides visual transformations, including deduplication and fuzzy matching of near-duplicate records, without code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redshift Spectrum: queries.
• Kinesis Analytics: streams.
• Lambda only: custom code.

Key takeaway: visual data cleaning → DataBrew.

stem: A dataset used for feature engineering is 20 TB in size and requires complex custom cleaning logic (multi-step joins, deduplication, and window functions) that exceeds what visual tools can easily express. Which AWS approach is best suited to perform this large-scale, code-driven data transformation before training?

choices.text: Apache Spark running on Amazon EMR
Amazon SageMaker Ground Truth
AWS Glue DataBrew's visual recipe builder only
Amazon Comprehend

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Spark on EMR scales complex custom cleaning logic over 20 TB.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ground Truth: labeling.
• DataBrew visual only: limited for complex custom logic at this scale.
• Comprehend: NLP.

Key takeaway: large custom processing → Spark on EMR.

stem: A data scientist is preparing numeric features for a model sensitive to feature scale. One feature ranges from 0 to 1,000,000 while another ranges from 0 to 1. The scientist wants to transform features to have zero mean and unit variance. Which technique should be applied?

choices.text: Standardization (z-score scaling)
Min-max normalization
Binning into quantiles
One-hot encoding

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Standardization (z-score) centers features and scales by standard deviation, handling differing scales and being less sensitive to outliers than min-max.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Min-max: sensitive to outliers.
• Binning: loses precision.
• One-hot: categorical.

Key takeaway: scale-sensitive models → standardization.

stem: A churn model uses customer age. Analysts believe risk changes in steps around life stages, and the model must be easy to explain per segment. Which transformation fits?

choices.text: Binning age into meaningful ranges
Tokenizing age into characters
Standardizing age with a z-score
One-hot encoding every distinct age

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Binning converts a continuous feature into categories, capturing step-like effects and producing segments that are easy to explain.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Z-score: rescales but keeps age continuous.
• Tokenizing: meant for text.
• One-hot per age: very sparse and hard to explain.

Key takeaway: step effects and explainable segments → binning.

stem: A team is preparing input features for a neural network that uses a sigmoid activation function in its input layer and performs best when all input features are scaled to a bounded range of 0 to 1. Which feature scaling technique directly achieves this bounded range?

choices.text: Log transformation only
Min-max normalization
Z-score standardization
Label encoding

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Min-max normalization maps features to a fixed range such as 0 to 1, matching a sigmoid's input and output range.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Log only: doesn't bound range.
• Z-score: unbounded.
• Label encoding: categorical.

Key takeaway: bounded ranges → min-max.

stem: A dataset feature contains a small number of extreme outliers alongside mostly well-behaved values. The team applies min-max normalization and finds that most values are compressed into a very narrow range near 0, reducing the feature's discriminative power for modeling. What is the best explanation and remedy for this issue?

choices.text: Min-max uses global min/max, so outliers dominate; use standard or robust scaling
Min-max isn't affected by outliers, so they must be data entry errors
This is expected, since normalization always compresses data this way
The issue comes from too many decimal places and is fixed by rounding

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Min-max uses the global min and max, so a few extreme outliers squash most values into a tiny range. Use standardization or robust scaling (or clip outliers).

Why the other options are wrong:
• Not affected by outliers: it is.
• Always compresses: not the issue.
• Decimal places: no.

Key takeaway: outliers break min-max scaling.

stem: A categorical feature 'color' has three unrelated values: 'red', 'green', 'blue'. If a data scientist uses label encoding (assigning 0, 1, 2) instead of one-hot encoding for this feature in a linear model, what is the main risk?

choices.text: It implies a false order between unrelated categories
One-hot encoding always performs worse than label encoding on any dataset
Label encoding cannot be applied to categorical string values at all
Label encoding uses more memory than one-hot encoding for this feature

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Label encoding assigns integers (0, 1, 2), implying an order between unrelated colors that models may misuse. One-hot avoids this.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One-hot always worse: no.
• Can't apply to strings: it can.
• More memory: label encoding uses less.

Key takeaway: nominal categories → one-hot, not labels.

stem: A categorical feature has 10,000 unique values (high cardinality), and one-hot encoding it would create an impractically wide and sparse feature matrix. Which encoding technique reduces dimensionality by representing each category as a compact binary code across a smaller number of columns instead of one column per category?

choices.text: Standardization
One-hot encoding
Binary encoding
Tokenization

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Binary encoding represents 10,000 categories with about 14 binary columns, avoiding one-hot's huge sparsity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Standardization: numeric.
• One-hot: 10,000 columns.
• Tokenization: text.

Key takeaway: high cardinality → binary (or target/hash) encoding.

stem: Product reviews must be turned into model input for a text classifier, and emojis and punctuation matter for sentiment. Which first step fits?

choices.text: Label-encode each whole review into one integer ID per unique review
Min-max normalize the review text length
Tokenize the text, keeping emojis and punctuation
One-hot encode each unique review string

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tokenization splits text into units such as words, subwords, or symbols that models can map to vectors. Choosing a tokenizer that keeps sentiment-bearing emojis and punctuation preserves signal.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Label-encoding reviews: every review becomes an unrelated ID.
• Length normalization: discards content.
• One-hot unique reviews: no generalization.

Key takeaway: text → tokens → vectors.

stem: A dataset includes a categorical feature representing education level with a natural order: 'high school' < 'bachelor's' < 'master's' < 'doctorate'. Which encoding approach best preserves this inherent ordering for a model that can benefit from ordinal relationships?

choices.text: One-hot encoding, because it always preserves order
Tokenization of each category name
Ordinal encoding with integers in natural order
Binary encoding without regard to category order

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Ordinal encoding assigns integers in the natural order (high school < bachelor's < master's < doctorate), preserving it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One-hot preserves order: it doesn't.
• Tokenization: text.
• Binary ignoring order: loses order.

Key takeaway: ordered categories → ordinal encoding.

stem: A team needs serverless Spark ETL that runs nightly, discovers new tables, processes only new files since the last run, and fails if data quality rules break. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Athena CTAS queries run on a schedule
AWS Lambda functions processing each file
AWS Glue jobs, crawlers, and bookmarks
Amazon EMR on a permanently running cluster

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue runs serverless Spark jobs, crawlers discover schemas, job bookmarks track processed data, and Glue Data Quality rules can fail or route jobs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Permanent EMR: servers to run and idle cost.
• Lambda: time and memory limits for large ETL.
• Athena CTAS: SQL transforms without bookmarks or rule-based failing.

Key takeaway: serverless Spark ETL with incremental loads → Glue.

stem: A business analyst without Spark or programming experience needs to explore a dataset, apply cleaning transformations interactively, and preview results before finalizing a recipe. A data engineer separately needs to build a production Spark-based ETL pipeline joining multiple large datasets with custom logic. Which pairing correctly matches each need to the appropriate AWS Glue capability?

choices.text: Both needs should be met with Amazon Athena's SQL-only interface
Both should use Glue Studio's visual editor only
The analyst writes PySpark; the engineer uses DataBrew to generate production code
DataBrew for the analyst; Glue ETL (Spark) for the engineer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DataBrew suits the analyst with no-code visual preparation, and Glue ETL (Spark) suits the engineer building scalable pipelines.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Athena for both: not preparation tooling.
• Glue Studio for both: less suited to the analyst's exploration.
• Swapped: analyst can't write PySpark.

Key takeaway: match the tool to the user.

stem: An ML engineering team needs full control over cluster configuration (instance types, Spark version, custom libraries, and long-running interactive Spark sessions) to process petabyte-scale training data with custom Scala Spark code. Which AWS service gives them the most control over the underlying Spark cluster environment?

choices.text: Amazon EMR running Apache Spark
AWS Glue ETL jobs (serverless Spark)
AWS Glue DataBrew
Amazon Athena

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EMR gives full control over cluster configuration, instance types, and Spark versions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Glue ETL: serverless with limited control.
• DataBrew: no-code.
• Athena: queries.

Key takeaway: full Spark control → EMR.

stem: New partitioned data lands daily in S3, sometimes with new columns. Athena and SageMaker need the tables updated automatically without breaking existing queries. Which setup fits?

choices.text: A manual ALTER TABLE run by an analyst each morning
A Glue DataBrew recipe applied to each new file
A Glue Studio visual job that rewrites the files daily
A scheduled Glue crawler updating the Data Catalog

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Crawlers infer schemas and add new partitions and columns to the Data Catalog. Their schema change policy controls how updates are applied, keeping tables current for Athena and other consumers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Visual job: transforms data but doesn't maintain the catalog by itself.
• DataBrew: data prep recipes.
• Manual ALTER: error-prone and slow.

Key takeaway: keep the catalog current → crawlers (or partition projection).

stem: A team must label 500,000 images with bounding boxes at lower cost, using a private workforce for sensitive images and automatically labeling easy images. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels training
Amazon Mechanical Turk directly, without any labeling tooling
SageMaker Ground Truth with automated labeling
SageMaker Data Wrangler transforms

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Ground Truth supports bounding-box tasks, private or vendor workforces, and automated data labeling that uses active learning to label confident items automatically, reducing cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Rekognition Custom Labels: trains models; it needs labels.
• Data Wrangler: data prep, not labeling.
• Raw Mechanical Turk: public workforce, unsuitable for sensitive data, and no automation.

Key takeaway: labeling at scale → Ground Truth.

stem: A healthcare company needs to label sensitive medical images and cannot use a public crowdsourced workforce due to data privacy requirements, but wants a managed labeling workflow with a private, vetted workforce of employees. Which Ground Truth workforce option satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: A private workforce composed of the company's own employees or invited members
Ground Truth does not support any workforce restrictions
A third-party vendor workforce found only through the AWS Marketplace, with no privacy controls
Amazon Mechanical Turk public workforce

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Ground Truth supports a private workforce of your own employees or invited members, keeping sensitive data off public crowds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• No restrictions: private workforces exist.
• Marketplace vendors only: optional, with privacy terms.
• Mechanical Turk: public.

Key takeaway: sensitive labeling → private workforce.

stem: A team using SageMaker Ground Truth for a large labeling job wants to reduce the total cost and time spent by human labelers without sacrificing overall label quality. Which built-in Ground Truth feature automatically labels a subset of data using a trained model and routes only low-confidence examples to human reviewers?

choices.text: SageMaker Clarify bias detection
Automated data labeling (active learning)
Ground Truth Plus fully outsourced labeling only
Manual review with no automation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automated data labeling uses active learning to label confident items automatically and sends uncertain ones to humans, cutting cost and time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Clarify: bias.
• Ground Truth Plus only: different offering.
• Manual only: costly.

Key takeaway: cheaper large labeling → automated labeling.

stem: A fraud model on data with 1% fraud reports 99% accuracy but catches almost no fraud. Which diagnosis and metric fit?

choices.text: Class imbalance; judge by recall, precision, PR-AUC
Label leakage; remove the most important feature
Underfitting; add more layers and train the model for longer
Data drift; retrain the model every week

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With 1% positives, predicting 'not fraud' always scores 99% accuracy. Metrics focused on the positive class (recall, precision, PR-AUC) reveal real performance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Drift: nothing indicates changing data.
• Leakage: would inflate fraud detection, not hide it.
• Underfitting: not indicated by the symptoms.

Key takeaway: imbalanced data → don't trust accuracy.

stem: Before training a model, an ML engineer wants to quantify how unevenly a sensitive facet (such as a demographic group) is represented in the training dataset, using a standardized pre-training bias metric. Which SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias metric directly measures this disparity in group representation?

choices.text: Difference in Positive Proportions in Labels (DPL)
Conditional Demographic Disparity in Predicted Labels (CDDPL)
Class Imbalance (CI)
Kullback-Leibler Divergence (KL) on model predictions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Class Imbalance (CI) measures how unevenly facet groups are represented in the dataset before training.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DPL: label proportions.
• CDDPL: predicted labels (post-training).
• KL on predictions: post-training.

Key takeaway: facet representation → CI.

stem: A model trained on a highly imbalanced dataset (95% negative class) shows 95% accuracy but a very low recall for the positive class, which is the class of business interest. What most likely explains this outcome, and which metric would better reveal the problem during evaluation?

choices.text: Imbalance favors the majority; use recall, precision, F1, or AUC-PR
The learning rate is too high; lowering it will fix the imbalance
The model overfits to noise; more training epochs will fix it
The dataset needs more features, not different evaluation metrics

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With 95% negatives, predicting all negatives scores 95% accuracy. Use recall, precision, F1, or PR AUC, and address imbalance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Learning rate: not the issue.
• More epochs: doesn't fix imbalance.
• More features: not the problem.

Key takeaway: imbalanced data → metrics beyond accuracy.

stem: A dataset has 2,000 minority and 200,000 majority examples. The team wants balanced training without discarding data or overfitting on duplicates. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Remove the minority class and train one-class
Duplicate minority rows 100 times before splitting
Randomly undersample the majority to 2,000
SMOTE or class weights on the training split

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SMOTE generates synthetic minority examples, and class weights make errors on the minority class cost more. Applying them only to the training split avoids leakage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Undersampling to 2,000: discards 99% of the majority data.
• Duplication before splitting: overfitting and leakage into validation.
• One-class: throws away labeled minority data.

Key takeaway: rebalance on training data only, preferring synthesis or weights.

stem: Rather than simply duplicating existing minority-class records, a data scientist wants to generate new, synthetic minority-class examples by interpolating between existing minority-class data points and their nearest neighbors in feature space. Which well-known technique does this describe?

choices.text: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)
Random undersampling
SMOTE (Synthetic Minority Over-sampling Technique)
One-hot encoding

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SMOTE creates synthetic minority examples by interpolating between neighbors, rather than duplicating records.

Why the other options are wrong:
• PCA: dimensionality.
• Undersampling: removes majority data.
• One-hot: encoding.

Key takeaway: synthetic minority samples → SMOTE.

stem: A team is choosing between oversampling the minority class and undersampling the majority class to correct imbalance in a dataset with only 500 total records, of which 20 are minority-class. Which trade-off should most influence their decision?

choices.text: Both produce identical models regardless of dataset size, so it doesn't matter
Undersampling is preferred
Oversample/SMOTE; undersampling would discard scarce data
Oversampling always causes underfitting, so undersampling is preferred

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With limited data, oversampling or SMOTE keeps all examples. Undersampling would discard scarce data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identical models: no.
• Undersampling preferred: loses data.
• Oversampling always underfits: no.

Key takeaway: small datasets → don't throw data away.

stem: A training dataset in S3 contains sensitive data. Security requires encryption at rest with a key only the ML team's roles can use, logged key usage, and encrypted training output. Which approach fits?

choices.text: SSE-KMS with a CMK, set as the job's output key
S3 Versioning with MFA Delete on the bucket
S3 Transfer Acceleration so uploads use encrypted edge paths
SSE-S3 default encryption on the input bucket

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A customer managed KMS key lets the key policy restrict usage to specific roles, with CloudTrail logging key use. SageMaker jobs can use a KMS key for output artifacts and volumes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SSE-S3: encrypts, but no key-level access control or usage logs.
• Versioning/MFA Delete: protect against deletion, not reading.
• Transfer Acceleration: speed only.

Key takeaway: control who can decrypt → a customer managed key.

stem: A dataset used for training contains customer names and full credit card numbers that are not needed as predictive features. Before storing the data for ML use, the team wants to irreversibly remove or obscure this sensitive information rather than merely restrict access to it. Which technique should be applied?

choices.text: IAM bucket policies alone
EBS Provisioned IOPS volumes
S3 Transfer Acceleration
Masking or anonymizing the sensitive fields

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Masking or anonymizing unneeded PII (names, card numbers) removes sensitive data from the training set.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM alone: data remains.
• EBS IOPS: unrelated.
• Transfer Acceleration: unrelated.

Key takeaway: remove unneeded PII before training.

stem: An ML engineering team is deciding how to protect personally identifiable information (PII) fields in a dataset that data scientists still need to analyze in aggregate but should not view individually. Which statement correctly distinguishes encryption from masking/anonymization in this context?

choices.text: Encryption applies only to data in transit, never to data at rest
Masking always requires a decryption key, just like encryption
Encryption and masking are functionally identical for this use case
Encryption is reversible with a key; masking irreversibly hides PII

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Encryption is reversible with the key. Masking irreversibly hides values, which suits fields the model doesn't need to recover.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Encryption only in transit: no.
• Masking needs keys: no.
• Identical: no.

Key takeaway: reversible vs. irreversible protection.

stem: A US health app's ML team processes diagnosis codes and claims linked to patients, and the company is a HIPAA covered entity. What does this data category require on AWS?

choices.text: PHI: BAA, eligible services, encryption
It's anonymous statistics, since codes aren't names
It's public data, so no special handling is needed
It's regulated only if stored outside the US

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Health data linked to individuals is protected health information. On AWS, covered entities sign a BAA, use HIPAA-eligible services, and apply safeguards such as encryption, access control, and logging.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Public or anonymous: codes linked to patients identify health information.
• Location-based: HIPAA applies regardless of storage location.

Key takeaway: PHI → BAA + eligible services + safeguards.

stem: An organization must ensure that customer training data for an EU-based product never leaves the European Union due to data residency regulations. Which AWS practice directly helps satisfy this requirement when architecting the ML data pipeline?

choices.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration for faster uploads within the EU
EU Regions only, enforced with SCPs
Use Amazon CloudFront to cache the data globally
Store data in any Region and rely on encryption for residency

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Keep data in EU Regions only and enforce it with SCPs denying other Regions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Transfer Acceleration: speed.
• CloudFront global caching: moves data out.
• Encryption for residency: doesn't keep data in place.

Key takeaway: data residency → Region restrictions via SCP.

stem: During an audit, a company discovers that a dataset containing customer Social Security numbers was used directly as a raw feature in a deployed ML model without any anonymization, violating internal PII handling policy. Which set of actions best addresses both the immediate compliance gap and prevents recurrence?

choices.text: Remove or mask the PII, retrain, and add Macie and data quality checks
Add a code comment documenting the issue without changing the pipeline
Do nothing, since the model performs well and retraining is costly
Encrypt the existing model artifact without changing the training data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Remove or mask the SSNs, retrain the model on clean data, and add controls such as Macie scanning and data quality checks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Comment only: no fix.
• Do nothing: compliance risk.
• Encrypt model only: data issue remains.

Key takeaway: fix the data, retrain, and prevent recurrence.

stem: A lender must explain individual predictions to regulators and check whether approval rates differ across age groups before and after training. Which tool fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Debugger
SageMaker Model Monitor data quality
Amazon Comprehend
SageMaker Clarify

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clarify computes pre- and post-training bias metrics and feature attributions (SHAP) for individual predictions, and can monitor both in production with Model Monitor.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Debugger: training internals such as gradients.
• Data quality monitor: distribution drift, not bias or explanations.
• Comprehend: text analytics.

Key takeaway: bias + explainability → Clarify.

stem: A team runs SageMaker Clarify twice: once on the raw training dataset before any model is built, and once after evaluating a trained model's predictions. What is the key difference between these two analysis phases?

choices.text: Pre-training metrics check the dataset; post-training check predictions
Post-training bias metrics can be computed only manually outside SageMaker
Pre-training metrics work only on images; post-training only on tabular data
No difference; Clarify supports only one type of bias analysis

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Pre-training bias metrics analyze the dataset itself. Post-training metrics analyze the trained model's predictions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Post-training manual only: Clarify computes them.
• Image/text split: no.
• No difference: two types exist.

Key takeaway: data bias vs. prediction bias.

stem: A pipeline must stop before training if more than 1% of rows have null customer IDs or if the label column has unexpected values. Which approach fits with the least code?

choices.text: Glue Data Quality rules (DQDL) as a pipeline gate
CloudWatch alarms on the S3 bucket's size and object count
Manual checks in a notebook before each run
Model Monitor data quality on the training data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Glue Data Quality lets you declare rules such as completeness and allowed values in DQDL and act on results, failing jobs or routing data, before training.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual checks: not automated.
• Model Monitor: monitors endpoints, not pipeline gates.
• Bucket size: says nothing about data quality.

Key takeaway: declarative data checks → Glue Data Quality.

stem: Before building a feature engineering pipeline, a data scientist wants a quick visual profile of a new dataset showing value distributions, missing value counts, and potential data quality issues such as duplicate rows, without writing any code. Which AWS Glue DataBrew capability provides this?

choices.text: DataBrew data profiling jobs
Glue Studio job bookmarks
DataBrew recipe job scheduling only
Glue Data Catalog table versioning

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DataBrew profiling jobs produce visual profiles of distributions, missing values, and correlations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Job bookmarks: incremental processing.
• Recipe scheduling: transformations.
• Catalog versioning: schemas.

Key takeaway: quick data profiles → DataBrew profiling.

stem: A churn model uses 80 numeric and categorical features on 2 million rows. The team needs strong accuracy quickly, handling of missing values, and feature importance. Which algorithm fits BEST as a first choice?

choices.text: A deep convolutional neural network
SageMaker XGBoost (gradient-boosted trees)
K-means clustering on the features to find churners
DeepAR forecasting

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gradient-boosted trees such as XGBoost are strong baselines for tabular data, handle missing values natively, and provide feature importance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CNN: designed for images.
• K-means: unsupervised; it doesn't predict churn.
• DeepAR: time-series forecasting.

Key takeaway: tabular supervised → gradient-boosted trees first.

stem: A company wants to automatically convert recorded customer service phone calls into text transcripts, including speaker labels, so that a downstream NLP model can analyze sentiment. Which AWS service should be used to generate the transcripts with minimal development effort?

choices.text: Amazon Comprehend
Amazon Translate
Amazon Polly
Amazon Transcribe

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Amazon Transcribe converts speech in recordings into text.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Comprehend: text analysis.
• Translate: languages.
• Polly: text to speech.

Key takeaway: speech to text → Transcribe.

stem: A media company wants to automatically flag user-uploaded images that contain explicit or suggestive content before they are published, without training a custom computer vision model. Which AWS service provides this capability out of the box?

choices.text: Amazon Textract
Amazon Rekognition
Amazon Comprehend
Amazon SageMaker semantic segmentation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Rekognition content moderation detects explicit or suggestive content in images.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Textract: documents.
• Comprehend: text.
• Semantic segmentation: custom model effort.

Key takeaway: image moderation → Rekognition.

stem: An app must translate support tickets into English in real time and apply company-specific terms consistently (product names must not be translated). Which approach fits?

choices.text: Amazon Comprehend with custom entity recognition
Amazon Transcribe with custom vocabularies
A seq2seq model trained from scratch on SageMaker
Amazon Translate with custom terminology

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Translate provides real-time neural translation, and custom terminology keeps specific terms, such as product names, translated (or untranslated) exactly as defined.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Comprehend: analysis, not translation.
• Transcribe: speech to text.
• Training from scratch: slow and costly.

Key takeaway: translation with controlled terms → Translate + custom terminology.

stem: A startup wants to add a generative text feature to its application that can summarize documents and answer questions, and wants to avoid provisioning GPU infrastructure or training a foundation model from scratch. Which approach best meets this requirement?

choices.text: Invoke a foundation model through Amazon Bedrock
Train a custom transformer model using SageMaker script mode
Build a SageMaker built-in Seq2Seq model
Deploy an open-source LLM on self-managed EC2 GPU instances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Invoking a foundation model through Bedrock adds summarization without training or managing infrastructure.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Custom transformer: heavy.
• Seq2Seq built-in: needs training data.
• Self-managed LLM on EC2: operations burden.

Key takeaway: GenAI features fast → Bedrock.

stem: A financial institution is choosing between a logistic regression model and a deep neural network for a loan approval decision that must be explained to regulators and applicants. Both models achieve similar accuracy on the validation set. Which factor should MOST influence the choice of model?

choices.text: The deep neural network always generalizes better on unseen data
The DNN needs no feature engineering
Logistic regression is easier to explain to regulators
The logistic regression model cannot be deployed on SageMaker endpoints

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Logistic regression is more interpretable, making decisions easier to explain to regulators.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DNN always generalizes better: no.
• DNN needs no feature engineering: not the point.
• Can't deploy on SageMaker: it can.

Key takeaway: regulated decisions → interpretable models.

stem: An operations team wants to detect unusual spikes in server request rates within a time series of metrics, without labeled examples of what constitutes 'anomalous' behavior. Which SageMaker built-in algorithm is designed for this task?

choices.text: Random Cut Forest
Factorization Machines
Linear Learner
K-Means

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Random Cut Forest detects anomalies such as unusual spikes in time series without labels.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Factorization Machines: sparse recommendation.
• Linear Learner: supervised.
• K-Means: clustering.

Key takeaway: unsupervised anomaly detection → RCF.

stem: A team wants to try several pretrained open models for text classification, fine-tune one on its data, and deploy it with one click, in its own account. Which capability fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Feature Store
SageMaker Ground Truth
SageMaker JumpStart
SageMaker Neo

explanation:
Why this is correct:
JumpStart provides a catalog of pretrained models and solution templates that can be fine-tuned and deployed to endpoints in your account.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ground Truth: labeling.
• Feature Store: features.
• Neo: compilation for hardware.

Key takeaway: pretrained model catalog + fine-tune + deploy → JumpStart.

stem: A team needs to train word embeddings efficiently on a large text corpus for downstream text classification, and separately needs to learn embeddings that capture relationships between pairs of arbitrary objects such as customer-product pairs. Which pairing of SageMaker built-in algorithms matches these two needs respectively?

choices.text: Both tasks should use Object2Vec
BlazingText for words; Object2Vec for pairs
Object2Vec for words; BlazingText for pairs
Both tasks should use BlazingText

explanation:
Why this is correct:
BlazingText trains word embeddings efficiently. Object2Vec learns embeddings for pairs of objects such as sentence pairs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Object2Vec for both: less efficient for words.
• Swapped: incorrect.
• BlazingText for pairs: not its purpose.

Key takeaway: words → BlazingText; pairs → Object2Vec.

stem: A team needs sentiment analysis on product reviews and has a tight budget with no in-house ML engineers. Which approach is generally the MOST cost-effective from a total-cost-of-ownership perspective?

choices.text: Provision a fleet of GPU instances to train a transformer from scratch
Hire additional ML engineers to build a bespoke solution
Build and train a custom SageMaker model, tuning hyperparameters with Automatic Model Tuning
Call Amazon Comprehend's sentiment analysis API

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Comprehend's sentiment API provides sentiment analysis with no ML expertise or training.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GPU fleet: costly.
• Hiring engineers: costly.
• Custom model: unnecessary.

Key takeaway: standard NLP task → managed AI service.

stem: An e-commerce company wants to predict the likelihood that a user will click on a specific product ad, using sparse, high-dimensional categorical features such as user ID and item ID. Which SageMaker built-in algorithm is specifically designed to handle this type of sparse high-cardinality data efficiently?

choices.text: Factorization Machines
Linear Learner
Semantic Segmentation
DeepAR

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Factorization Machines model interactions in sparse, high-dimensional data such as user-item click prediction.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Linear Learner: misses interactions.
• Semantic segmentation: images.
• DeepAR: forecasting.

Key takeaway: sparse click prediction → Factorization Machines.

stem: A manufacturing company needs to identify the exact pixel-level boundaries of defects on product images captured on an assembly line, rather than just detecting whether a defect is present. Which SageMaker built-in algorithm is most appropriate?

choices.text: Semantic Segmentation
Object Detection
BlazingText
Image Classification

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Semantic segmentation labels each pixel, giving exact defect boundaries.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Object detection: bounding boxes.
• BlazingText: text.
• Image classification: whole-image labels.

Key takeaway: pixel-level boundaries → semantic segmentation.

stem: A retailer must forecast demand for 20,000 related products, including new products with little history, and provide prediction intervals for inventory planning. Which approach fits?

choices.text: DeepAR with quantile forecasts
K-means clustering of historical sales
XGBoost predicting only point estimates
A separate linear regression per product

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DeepAR trains one model across many related time series, which helps cold-start items, and produces probabilistic (quantile) forecasts for intervals.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Per-product regression: poor for sparse or new items and no intervals.
• K-means: groups items; doesn't forecast.
• Point estimates only: no intervals.

Key takeaway: many related series + intervals → DeepAR.

stem: A team wants to use a novel research algorithm that is not available among SageMaker's built-in algorithms, and needs full control over the training code and dependencies. Which SageMaker training approach should they choose compared to using a built-in algorithm?

choices.text: Use SageMaker JumpStart and select a pretrained model
Bring their own Docker container with custom training code
Use the built-in Linear Learner algorithm and adjust hyperparameters
Use SageMaker Autopilot to automatically select an algorithm

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bringing your own Docker container lets you run any custom training code on SageMaker.

Why the other options are wrong:
• JumpStart: pretrained models.
• Linear Learner: different algorithm.
• Autopilot: chooses among standard algorithms.

Key takeaway: custom algorithms → bring your own container.

stem: A retailer has only a few hundred labeled images of its specific product packaging and wants to build an image classifier to detect counterfeit packaging, with minimal ML expertise and development time. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

choices.text: Rekognition Custom Labels on the small set
Train a CNN from scratch in SageMaker script mode
Use Amazon Comprehend to classify the images
Hand-engineer pixel features for logistic regression

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Rekognition Custom Labels trains a custom image model from a few hundred labeled images using transfer learning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CNN from scratch: needs more data and expertise.
• Comprehend: text.
• Hand-engineered features: poor accuracy.

Key takeaway: small custom image datasets → Custom Labels.

stem: A factory needs to know which of 12 defect types appear anywhere in an image (several can appear at once), without locating them. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Object detection with bounding boxes
Semantic segmentation per pixel
BlazingText on image file names
Multi-label image classification

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Image classification assigns labels to the whole image, and multi-label mode supports several labels per image. Locations aren't required here.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Object detection: adds localization that isn't needed.
• Segmentation: pixel-level, even more than needed.
• BlazingText: for text.

Key takeaway: what's in the image (no location) → classification.

stem: Training uses 1,000,000 examples with batch size 500 for 10 epochs. How many weight updates occur, and what is one epoch?

choices.text: 2,000 updates; an epoch is one layer
10 updates; an epoch is one weight update
500 updates; an epoch is one batch
20,000 updates; an epoch is one full pass

explanation:
Why this is correct:
One epoch processes the full dataset once. Here that's 1,000,000 / 500 = 2,000 batches (updates) per epoch, so 10 epochs give 20,000 updates.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One update per epoch: that would be full-batch training.
• One batch per epoch: confuses batch with epoch.
• Layer-based: epochs aren't related to layers.

Key takeaway: updates = (examples / batch size) × epochs.

stem: A data scientist is training a deep learning model on a SageMaker GPU training instance and repeatedly encounters an out-of-memory error during training. The model architecture and dataset are fixed. Which change is MOST likely to resolve the issue without changing instance type?

choices.text: Add more convolutional layers to the model
Increase the learning rate
Increase the number of epochs
Reduce the batch size

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GPU out-of-memory errors during training are usually fixed by reducing the batch size.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More layers: more memory.
• Higher learning rate: unrelated.
• More epochs: unrelated.

Key takeaway: GPU OOM → smaller batch.

stem: Validation loss stops improving after epoch 12 of 100, and training continues to reduce training loss. The team wants to save cost and keep the best model. Which technique fits?

choices.text: More training epochs to reach convergence
A higher learning rate for the final epochs to escape the plateau
Early stopping with checkpoint of the best epoch
Removing the validation set to use more data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Early stopping ends training when the validation metric stops improving for a set patience, saving compute and avoiding overfitting. Keeping the best checkpoint retains the best model. SageMaker tuning jobs can also stop weak jobs early.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Higher learning rate: likely worsens things.
• More epochs: more overfitting and cost.
• No validation set: loses the stopping signal.

Key takeaway: stop on validation plateau; keep the best checkpoint.

stem: A team is training an extremely large language model whose parameters do not fit in the memory of a single GPU, even with a batch size of one. Which distributed training strategy directly addresses this specific constraint?

choices.text: Data parallelism, which replicates the full model on each device and splits the data
Reducing the number of training epochs
Model parallelism, which splits the model itself across multiple devices
Increasing the batch size on a single GPU

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model parallelism splits the model's layers or tensors across multiple GPUs when parameters don't fit in one GPU's memory.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data parallelism: replicates the full model.
• Fewer epochs: unrelated.
• Bigger batch: more memory.

Key takeaway: model too big for one GPU → model parallelism.

stem: A large neural network overfits: 99% training accuracy, 78% validation. The team wants a regularization technique applied during training that randomly disables neurons. Which is it, and when is it active?

choices.text: Data augmentation, applied to the weights
Dropout, active only during training
Early stopping, applied to individual neurons
Batch normalization, active only during inference

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Dropout randomly zeroes a fraction of activations during training, which forces redundancy and reduces overfitting. At inference, all neurons are used.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Batch normalization: normalizes activations; not random deactivation.
• Early stopping: stops training; not per neuron.
• Data augmentation: changes input data, not weights.

Key takeaway: dropout = training-time random deactivation.

stem: A team wants a regularization technique that tends to drive some model weights to exactly zero, effectively performing feature selection, as opposed to shrinking all weights toward small but nonzero values. Which regularization approach should they use?

choices.text: Dropout
Early stopping
L1 regularization
L2 regularization (weight decay)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
L1 regularization drives some weights to exactly zero, effectively selecting features.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dropout: randomly drops units.
• Early stopping: stops training.
• L2: shrinks weights but rarely to zero.

Key takeaway: sparse weights → L1.

stem: A team wants to efficiently search a large hyperparameter space for an XGBoost model on SageMaker, using a strategy that learns from previous training job results to select more promising hyperparameter combinations, rather than testing combinations randomly or exhaustively. Which SageMaker capability and strategy should they use?

choices.text: SageMaker Autopilot with random hyperparameter selection
SageMaker Debugger to search hyperparameters
SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning using the Bayesian search strategy
SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning using only the grid search strategy

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automatic Model Tuning with Bayesian search uses previous results to choose promising hyperparameters, searching efficiently.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Autopilot random: not the tool.
• Debugger: training issues.
• Grid search only: inefficient for large spaces.

Key takeaway: efficient hyperparameter search → Bayesian tuning.

stem: A team has already run a SageMaker hyperparameter tuning job for a model and now wants to run a new tuning job with a slightly expanded hyperparameter range, while reusing knowledge gained from the previous tuning job to converge faster. Which SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning feature should they use?

choices.text: SageMaker Model Registry versioning
Multi-model endpoints
Warm start tuning jobs
Early stopping for training jobs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Warm start tuning reuses results from previous tuning jobs to start a new search from prior knowledge.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Model Registry: models.
• Multi-model endpoints: hosting.
• Early stopping: individual jobs.

Key takeaway: build on earlier tuning → warm start.

stem: A team has a PyTorch training script with a custom loop and wants to run it on SageMaker with managed spot training and distributed data parallelism, without building a container. Which approach fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Autopilot with the script uploaded
A custom Docker image built from scratch
A SageMaker built-in algorithm that replaces the script
Script mode with the SageMaker PyTorch container

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Script mode runs your own training script in a prebuilt framework container, with SageMaker features such as spot training and distribution configured through the estimator.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Built-in algorithm: discards the custom code.
• Autopilot: AutoML; doesn't run your script.
• Custom image: unnecessary work here.

Key takeaway: own script + managed framework container → script mode.

stem: A company wants to adapt a foundation model available in Amazon Bedrock to better follow its brand's specific tone and terminology, using a set of labeled example prompts and responses, without managing any training infrastructure. Which Bedrock capability supports this goal?

choices.text: Increase the model's context window size manually
Switch to a larger foundation model without customization
Use Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels
Fine-tune the model on the labeled dataset

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fine-tuning the Bedrock model on the labeled examples teaches it the brand's style.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Context window: not customization.
• Larger model: no brand adaptation.
• Rekognition: images.

Key takeaway: style adaptation with labeled data → fine-tuning.

stem: During training, a model's training accuracy steadily increases to 99%, but its validation accuracy plateaus at 70% and then begins to decrease over further epochs. Which of the following is the MOST likely explanation and an appropriate remedy?

choices.text: The training set is too large; reducing it should help
Overfitting; add regularization or reduce complexity
The learning rate is too low; increasing it will close the gap
Underfitting; increasing model complexity should help

explanation:
Why this is correct:
High training accuracy with falling validation accuracy means overfitting. Add regularization, reduce complexity, or get more data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Training set too large: no.
• Raise learning rate: not the fix.
• Underfitting: opposite.

Key takeaway: train up, validation down → overfitting.

stem: A regression model shows high error on both the training set and the validation set, and the error does not improve significantly even after training for many more epochs. Which of the following changes is MOST likely to help?

choices.text: Apply stronger L2 weight decay
Reduce the size of the training dataset
Add more dropout layers to reduce overfitting
Increase capacity; it's underfitting

explanation:
Why this is correct:
High error on both training and validation means underfitting. Increase model capacity or improve features.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Stronger L2: worsens underfitting.
• Less data: worse.
• More dropout: worsens underfitting.

Key takeaway: high error everywhere → underfitting.

stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes bagging from boosting as ensemble learning techniques?

choices.text: Bagging and boosting are two names for exactly the same technique
Bagging trains sequentially on errors; boosting trains independently in parallel
Bagging: parallel, reduces variance; boosting: sequential, reduces bias
Bagging works only with neural networks, boosting only with trees

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bagging trains models in parallel on bootstrapped data to reduce variance. Boosting trains sequentially on previous errors to reduce bias.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same technique: no.
• Swapped: incorrect.
• Model-type restrictions: no.

Key takeaway: bagging = parallel/variance; boosting = sequential/bias.

stem: A team needs to deploy a large trained deep learning model to a resource-constrained edge device and must reduce the model's size and inference latency, accepting a small, controlled loss in accuracy. Which technique is specifically designed to achieve this by reducing the numerical precision of the model's weights?

choices.text: Adding more hidden layers
Quantization
Using a larger batch size during training
Increasing the number of training epochs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Quantization lowers numeric precision (for example, to int8), shrinking the model and speeding inference on edge devices.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More layers: bigger.
• Larger batch: training only.
• More epochs: training only.

Key takeaway: edge deployment → quantization.

stem: Models must be versioned, approved by a reviewer, and deployed automatically only when approved, with lineage to the training job. Which capability fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Feature Store
An S3 bucket with a folder per model version
Amazon ECR image tags
Model Registry with approval status

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model Registry groups model versions (model packages) with metadata and lineage. Approval status changes emit events that can trigger deployment pipelines.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 folders: no approval workflow.
• Feature Store: features, not models.
• ECR tags: images, not model approval.

Key takeaway: versioned, approved models → Model Registry.

stem: A model's weights grow very large and it overfits. The team adds a term to the loss equal to λ times the sum of squared weights. What is this, and what is its effect?

choices.text: L2 regularization (weight decay); smaller weights
Dropout; disables neurons at random
Learning rate decay; slows training over time
L1 regularization; forces weights to exactly zero

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Weight decay (L2) penalizes squared weights, shrinking them and reducing overfitting. L1 penalizes absolute values and tends to produce sparse weights.

Why the other options are wrong:
• L1: absolute-value penalty.
• Dropout: random deactivation, not a loss term.
• Learning rate decay: changes step size, not the loss.

Key takeaway: squared penalty = L2; absolute = L1.

stem: A team wants to significantly reduce the wall-clock time needed to train a large model on a massive dataset, and has budget for additional compute instances. Which approach directly reduces training time by processing different portions of data in parallel across multiple instances?

choices.text: Reduce the size of the training dataset
Distributed data-parallel training
Switch from Adam to plain SGD
Increase the number of training epochs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Distributed data-parallel training splits data across many GPUs or instances, cutting wall-clock time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Less data: hurts accuracy.
• Plain SGD: not faster.
• More epochs: slower.

Key takeaway: faster training on big data → data parallelism.

stem: A medical screening model is being tuned to flag patients who may have a disease for further testing. Missing a true positive case (a false negative) is considered far more costly than incorrectly flagging a healthy patient (a false positive). Which metric should the team prioritize maximizing, even at some cost to the other?

choices.text: Training accuracy on the training set
Specificity of negative predictions only
Precision
Recall

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Recall measures how many actual positive cases are caught, which matters most when missing a disease is costly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Training accuracy: not the goal.
• Specificity: negatives.
• Precision: false positives.

Key takeaway: don't miss positives → recall.

stem: A spam classifier must balance false positives (lost emails) and false negatives (spam getting through) with one metric for model selection, on imbalanced data. Which metric fits?

choices.text: F1 score (harmonic mean of precision and recall)
R-squared of the predicted probabilities
Accuracy on the full test set, including both classes
RMSE of the predicted probabilities

explanation:
Why this is correct:
F1 combines precision and recall, and the harmonic mean penalizes a model that is strong on one but weak on the other. It suits imbalanced classification.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Accuracy: misleading with imbalance.
• RMSE and R-squared: regression metrics.

Key takeaway: one number balancing precision and recall → F1.

stem: A disease screening model flags 50 healthy patients as sick. What are these errors called, and which metric do they lower?

choices.text: False negatives; they lower recall
True positives; they lower accuracy
True negatives; they lower specificity
False positives; they lower precision

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Healthy people predicted positive are false positives. Precision = TP / (TP + FP), so more false positives lower precision.

Why the other options are wrong:
• False negatives: sick patients predicted healthy, which lower recall.
• True negatives: correct predictions.
• True positives: correct predictions.

Key takeaway: FP → precision; FN → recall.

stem: A delivery-time model will be judged mainly on avoiding large errors, since a few very late deliveries cost far more than many small errors. Which metric fits BEST?

choices.text: RMSE, which penalizes large errors more
MAE, which weighs every error equally regardless of size
AUC-ROC of the predictions
Accuracy of rounded predictions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RMSE squares errors before averaging, so large errors dominate the score. MAE treats all errors linearly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MAE: doesn't emphasize large errors.
• Accuracy and AUC: classification metrics.

Key takeaway: large errors costly → RMSE.

stem: A binary classifier produces an AUC-ROC score of 0.5 on a held-out test set. What does this score indicate about the model's performance?

choices.text: The model is highly overfit to the training data
The model perfectly separates the two classes
The model has a precision of exactly 50%
It's no better than random guessing

explanation:
Why this is correct:
AUC-ROC of 0.5 means the model ranks positives and negatives no better than random.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Overfit: not implied.
• Perfect separation: AUC 1.0.
• Precision 50%: different metric.

Key takeaway: AUC 0.5 = random.
