stem: A fraud detection model is trained on a dataset where only 0.5% of transactions are fraudulent. The model achieves 99.4% accuracy but fails to identify almost any actual fraud cases. Which evaluation approach would have surfaced this problem earlier?

choices.text: Precision, recall, and F1 on the fraud class
Report only overall accuracy on the full test set
Use a larger batch size during training
Increase the number of training epochs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With 0.5% fraud, use precision, recall, and F1 on the fraud class. Accuracy is misleading.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Accuracy only: misleading.
• Batch size: training.
• Epochs: training.

Key takeaway: rare positives → class-specific metrics.

stem: After training a binary classification model, a team wants to measure whether the model's false positive rates differ significantly between two demographic groups, as part of assessing fairness. Which SageMaker Clarify metric category addresses this?

choices.text: Feature importance metrics only
Post-training bias metrics
Model Debugger tensor metrics
Pre-training bias metrics

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Post-training bias metrics in Clarify measure whether the model's error rates, such as false positive rates, differ across groups.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Feature importance only: not bias.
• Debugger tensors: training internals.
• Pre-training metrics: data only.

Key takeaway: model outcome bias → post-training metrics.

stem: During training of a very deep neural network, a data scientist observes that the loss stops decreasing early and suspects that gradients in the earlier layers have become extremely small. Which SageMaker capability can automatically monitor tensors during training and trigger an alert when this specific condition (vanishing gradients) is detected?

choices.text: Debugger's vanishing gradient rule
SageMaker Clarify bias detection
Model Monitor data quality checks
Ground Truth active learning

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Debugger's vanishing gradient rule detects gradients shrinking toward zero, which stalls learning in deep networks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Clarify: bias.
• Model Monitor: deployed data.
• Ground Truth: labeling.

Key takeaway: training issues → Debugger rules.

stem: A deep training job occasionally diverges with exploding gradients after hours of compute. The team wants it detected automatically and the job stopped early to save cost. Which fits?

choices.text: CloudTrail events for the training job's API calls
Clarify bias reports on the model
Model Monitor schedules on the endpoint
Debugger built-in rules with a stop action

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Debugger captures tensors during training and evaluates rules such as exploding gradients or overfitting. Rule actions can stop the job and notify.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Clarify: bias and explainability.
• Model Monitor: production endpoints.
• CloudTrail: API calls.

Key takeaway: training health checks → Debugger rules.

stem: A team is evaluating a binary classifier on a dataset where the positive class represents only 1% of all examples. Which curve is generally considered more informative for comparing model performance in this heavily imbalanced setting, and why?

choices.text: Both curves are mathematically identical
The ROC curve, which is always superior regardless of class balance
Precision-recall, focused on the minority class
Neither is meaningful for imbalanced data; use accuracy only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
For a rare positive class, the precision-recall curve focuses on minority-class performance. ROC can look optimistic with many negatives.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Identical curves: no.
• ROC always superior: not for imbalance.
• Accuracy only: misleading.

Key takeaway: imbalanced evaluation → PR curves.

stem: A complex model reports 91% accuracy on a dataset where 90% of examples are one class. How should the team interpret this?

choices.text: Use the complex model as the baseline
91% shows the model is production-ready
Baselines are only needed for regression models, not classifiers
Compare to a majority-class baseline: only +1 point

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A trivial baseline that always predicts the majority class gets 90%, so the model adds only 1 point. Baselines show whether complexity is actually helping.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Production-ready: ignores the baseline.
• Regression only: baselines apply to all tasks.
• Complex model as baseline: defeats the purpose.

Key takeaway: always compare to a simple baseline.

stem: A binary classifier for a rare disease (prevalence 1%) is reported to have 99% accuracy. A stakeholder assumes this means the model is highly effective at identifying disease cases. What is the most likely flaw in this reasoning?

choices.text: 99% accuracy always implies near-perfect recall on the positive class
Accuracy isn't affected by class imbalance and is always reliable
Always predicting 'no disease' also scores ~99%
The model must also have a recall of exactly 99%

explanation:
Why this is correct:
With 1% prevalence, always predicting 'no disease' scores about 99% accuracy while catching no cases. Accuracy alone is misleading.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Implies recall: no.
• Unaffected by imbalance: false.
• Recall exactly 99%: not implied.

Key takeaway: check a trivial baseline.

stem: For a multi-class classification confusion matrix with three classes (A, B, C), how is the per-class precision for class A typically calculated?

choices.text: Correct A predictions divided by all actual class A instances
Instances actually in B or C that were predicted as class A
All correct predictions divided by all instances
Correct A predictions ÷ all predicted as A

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Per-class precision for A is correct A predictions divided by all instances predicted as A.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Divided by actual A: recall.
• B or C predicted as A: false positives only.
• All correct over all: accuracy.

Key takeaway: precision = TP / predicted positives.

stem: A model gets a few requests per hour with long idle gaps. The payload is 2 MB, a 2-second cold start is acceptable, and the team wants to pay nothing when idle. Which option fits?

choices.text: An asynchronous endpoint kept at one instance
A real-time endpoint on a GPU instance
Batch Transform triggered per request
SageMaker Serverless Inference

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Serverless Inference scales to zero and bills per request duration, with occasional cold starts, which fits sporadic traffic with small payloads.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Real-time GPU: pays while idle.
• Batch per request: slow and awkward for requests.
• Async with one instance: pays while idle (async can scale to zero, but a fixed instance defeats that).

Key takeaway: sporadic traffic, no idle cost → serverless.

stem: An ML engineer must deploy a model that processes individual requests with payloads up to 800 MB and inference times that can exceed 10 minutes per request. Immediate synchronous responses are not required, but requests must be queued and processed reliably as capacity becomes available. Which SageMaker inference option satisfies these requirements?

choices.text: A serverless inference endpoint
SageMaker Batch Transform
A real-time inference endpoint
An asynchronous inference endpoint

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Asynchronous inference accepts large payloads (up to 1 GB) through S3 and long processing times, queuing requests and notifying on completion.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Serverless: small payloads and short time limits.
• Batch Transform: offline datasets, not individual requests.
• Real-time: 6 MB payload and 60-second limits.

Key takeaway: large, slow single requests → asynchronous inference.

stem: Every night, 50 million rows in S3 need predictions written back to S3 before 6 AM. No real-time access is needed. Which option is MOST cost-effective?

choices.text: A real-time endpoint invoked 50 million times
A multi-model endpoint for the nightly job
Serverless Inference invoked per row
SageMaker Batch Transform over the dataset

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Batch Transform spins up instances, processes the whole dataset from S3 (with batching), writes results to S3, and shuts down, with no persistent endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Real-time endpoint: pays for always-on capacity and per-request overhead.
• Serverless per row: request overhead at huge scale.
• Multi-model endpoint: for many models, not bulk scoring.

Key takeaway: offline bulk scoring → Batch Transform.

stem: A company is deciding on compute for a real-time endpoint hosting a large transformer-based deep learning model where inference latency is critical. Choosing a GPU-backed instance over a CPU-backed instance for this endpoint primarily trades which two factors against each other?

choices.text: Lower model accuracy versus faster training time
Higher storage cost versus better data durability
Fewer IAM permissions versus simpler networking
Higher hourly cost for much lower latency

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GPU or accelerator instances cost more per hour but greatly reduce latency for large transformer inference.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Accuracy vs. training time: not the tradeoff.
• Storage vs. durability: unrelated.
• IAM vs. networking: unrelated.

Key takeaway: accelerated inference = cost for latency.

stem: A vision model must run on edge devices with ARM CPUs and limited memory, with lower latency than the framework runtime. Which capability fits?

choices.text: SageMaker JumpStart fine-tuning for smaller devices
SageMaker Neo compilation for the target hardware
SageMaker Clarify explainability
SageMaker Model Monitor

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Neo compiles trained models into optimized executables for specific hardware targets, including edge devices, improving latency and memory use.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Clarify: explainability.
• JumpStart: pretrained models.
• Model Monitor: production monitoring.

Key takeaway: hardware-optimized inference → Neo.

stem: A company trains and manages hundreds of similar per-customer models using the same framework and container image, but each customer's traffic is low and sporadic. To minimize hosting cost, they want a single endpoint that dynamically loads the appropriate model artifact from Amazon S3 only when it is invoked. Which SageMaker feature should they use?

choices.text: A multi-model endpoint
A multi-container endpoint
A serial inference pipeline
Separate real-time endpoints per customer

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A multi-model endpoint hosts many models with the same framework behind one endpoint, loading them from S3 on demand to save cost.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Multi-container: different containers, few models.
• Serial pipeline: chained steps.
• Endpoint per customer: costly.

Key takeaway: many similar models → multi-model endpoint.

stem: How does a SageMaker multi-container endpoint differ from a SageMaker multi-model endpoint?

choices.text: Multi-container: different containers invoked or chained; multi-model: many same-framework models
A multi-container endpoint retrains models automatically, while multi-model doesn't
Multi-container supports only batch; multi-model supports only real-time
No meaningful difference; the two terms are interchangeable

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A multi-container endpoint hosts different containers invoked directly or chained. A multi-model endpoint hosts many models sharing one container.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Retrains automatically: no.
• Batch vs. real-time: no.
• Interchangeable: no.

Key takeaway: different containers vs. many models in one container.

stem: A team already orchestrates SageMaker training, processing, and deployment steps and wants an orchestrator with native, low-friction integration to SageMaker-specific step types, such as model registration and conditional model approval, without standing up and managing separate orchestration infrastructure. Which option best fits, compared to using self-managed Apache Airflow on Amazon MWAA?

choices.text: AWS CodePipeline
AWS Step Functions
Amazon EventBridge
SageMaker Pipelines

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Pipelines orchestrates ML workflows (processing, training, evaluation, registration, deployment) with lineage tracking.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodePipeline: general CI/CD.
• Step Functions: general orchestration.
• EventBridge: events.

Key takeaway: ML workflow orchestration → SageMaker Pipelines.

stem: A custom inference container on SageMaker fails with 'container did not pass the ping health check'. Which TWO requirements must the container meet? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Serve predictions on POST /invocations
Write every prediction to Amazon Redshift
Run the container as the root user
Respond 200 to GET /ping when healthy
Expose a public static IP address

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker hosting sends health checks to GET /ping and inference requests to POST /invocations on port 8080. The container must answer both.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Static IP: SageMaker manages networking.
• Redshift writes: not required.
• Root user: not required.

Key takeaway: BYOC hosting contract = /ping + /invocations.

stem: A team hosts a high-throughput deep learning inference workload and wants to lower cost per inference while keeping latency low, without changing their model architecture. Which approach offers the best price-performance trade-off for this deep learning inference use case?

choices.text: Move the workload to SageMaker Batch Transform
Switch to a general-purpose CPU instance to cut cost
Compile with Neo and deploy on Inferentia
Add endpoint variants without changing instance type

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Compiling the model with SageMaker Neo and deploying on Inferentia lowers cost per inference for high-throughput deep learning.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Batch Transform: not real-time.
• CPU instances: slower for deep learning.
• More variants on same instance: no cost change.

Key takeaway: cheaper DL inference → Inferentia + Neo.

stem: A team wants to release a new model to a production endpoint gradually and roll back automatically if latency alarms fire, with no downtime. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A new EndpointConfig with deployment guardrails
Change the endpoint's IAM execution role
Delete the endpoint and create it again with the new model
Overwrite the model artifact in S3 in place

explanation:
Why this is correct:
UpdateEndpoint with a new endpoint configuration and deployment guardrails (canary or linear traffic shifting with alarm-based rollback) shifts traffic safely while the old fleet remains available.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete and recreate: downtime.
• Overwriting S3: not picked up safely and no rollback.
• IAM role: unrelated.

Key takeaway: safe model updates → new EndpointConfig + guardrails.

stem: A lightweight scikit-learn model, a few megabytes in size, needs to be invoked by a mobile application backend only a few times per minute, and the team wants to avoid managing any servers or SageMaker endpoints at all, paying only for actual invocations. Which deployment target is most appropriate?

choices.text: A Lambda function with the model, behind API Gateway
A SageMaker real-time endpoint on a large GPU instance
A dedicated EC2 instance running 24/7
SageMaker Batch Transform running continuously

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A small scikit-learn model can run inside a Lambda function behind API Gateway, paying only per request.

Why the other options are wrong:
• GPU endpoint: overkill.
• 24/7 EC2: idle cost.
• Continuous Batch Transform: not real-time.

Key takeaway: tiny models, low traffic → Lambda.

stem: A workload has steady, predictable SageMaker endpoint usage 24/7 for the next year. Which purchasing approach reduces compute cost compared to paying full on-demand rates, without requiring the workload to tolerate interruptions?

choices.text: Commit to a SageMaker Savings Plan for a 1- or 3-year term
Use SageMaker serverless inference for the steady workload
Use on-demand instances exclusively
Use SageMaker Managed Spot Training for hosting

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A SageMaker Savings Plan for a 1- or 3-year term discounts steady, predictable usage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Serverless for steady load: not cheapest.
• On-demand only: no discount.
• Spot training for hosting: not for endpoints.

Key takeaway: steady usage → Savings Plans.

stem: A team wants identical SageMaker endpoints in dev and prod, reviewed changes before deploy, and easy rollback of configuration. Which practice fits?

choices.text: Define model, config, and endpoint in versioned IaC
Create endpoints manually in the console each time
Hardcode endpoint settings in application code
Use a one-off CLI script that is then discarded

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Declaring SageMaker Model, EndpointConfig, and Endpoint resources in CloudFormation (or CDK) keeps environments consistent, lets change sets show diffs, and makes rollback a redeploy of a previous template version.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual console: drift.
• Hardcoded settings: not infrastructure management.
• Discarded script: not repeatable.

Key takeaway: ML infrastructure belongs in versioned IaC.

stem: A custom inference image must be stored privately, scanned for CVEs, protected from tag overwrites, and pulled by SageMaker. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon ECR with scanning and tag immutability
AWS Secrets Manager holding the image
Amazon S3 with the image stored as a tarball
AWS CodeArtifact as a private package and image repository

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker pulls custom images from ECR, which offers scanning and tag immutability.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 tarball: SageMaker doesn't run images from S3.
• CodeArtifact: language packages.
• Secrets Manager: secrets.

Key takeaway: container images → ECR.

stem: A real-time endpoint's traffic grows fivefold at noon. The team wants instance count to follow load within limits of 2-10. Which setup fits?

choices.text: An AWS Config rule that resizes the endpoint
Application Auto Scaling target tracking
A Trusted Advisor recommendation reviewed weekly
A CloudWatch dashboard watched by the team

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker endpoints scale through Application Auto Scaling, commonly with target tracking on SageMakerVariantInvocationsPerInstance and minimum and maximum capacity.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: compliance, not scaling.
• Weekly recommendation: manual and slow.
• Dashboard: observation only.

Key takeaway: endpoint scaling → Application Auto Scaling.

stem: A SageMaker endpoint configured with target-tracking auto scaling based on SageMakerVariantInvocationsPerInstance is scaling out too slowly during sudden traffic spikes, causing elevated latency for several minutes after each spike begins. Which adjustment would most directly address this?

choices.text: Increase the scale-in cooldown period
Remove auto scaling and use a fixed instance count
Shorten the scale-out cooldown
Scale on Amazon S3 storage utilization instead

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If scaling out lags spikes, shorten the scale-out cooldown so the endpoint adds instances sooner.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Longer scale-in cooldown: doesn't speed scale-out.
• Fixed count: loses elasticity.
• S3 utilization: unrelated.

Key takeaway: slow reaction to spikes → shorter scale-out cooldown.

stem: When configuring target-tracking auto scaling for a SageMaker real-time endpoint, which metric most directly reflects end-user response time and is often preferred over CPUUtilization for scaling decisions on latency-sensitive workloads?

choices.text: NetworkPacketsIn
MemoryReservation
DiskUtilization
ModelLatency

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ModelLatency reflects how long the model takes to respond, making it a meaningful scaling metric for latency-sensitive endpoints.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NetworkPacketsIn, MemoryReservation, DiskUtilization: not SageMaker endpoint scaling metrics for latency.

Key takeaway: scale on metrics that reflect user impact.

stem: A bank requires that a SageMaker endpoint be reachable only from its VPC and that model containers can reach only approved resources. Which TWO measures address this? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Remove the IAM execution role
Turn on Model Monitor data capture
Invoke via an interface VPC endpoint
Enable SageMaker Neo compilation for the endpoint
Deploy in the VPC with security groups

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Running the model in your VPC with security groups controls what its containers can reach, and invoking the runtime API through an interface VPC endpoint (optionally with an endpoint policy and source-VPC conditions) keeps calls private.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Neo: performance.
• No execution role: the model couldn't pull artifacts.
• Data capture: monitoring.

Key takeaway: private endpoints = VPC config + PrivateLink for invocation.

stem: In the SageMaker Python SDK, which call actually provisions a real-time endpoint and what does it create?

choices.text: estimator.fit(...); trains and deploys
sagemaker.Session(); provisions infrastructure
model.deploy(...); creates config and endpoint
estimator.transformer(...); creates an endpoint

explanation:
Why this is correct:
deploy creates the model (if needed), an endpoint configuration, and the endpoint with the requested instances.

Why the other options are wrong:
• fit: trains only.
• transformer: prepares batch transform.
• Session: a client helper.

Key takeaway: deploy = real-time hosting.

stem: A team wants to reduce the cost of a long-running SageMaker training job for a fault-tolerant deep learning model that can resume from checkpoints. Which approach reduces cost the most while accepting the risk of training interruptions?

choices.text: Managed Spot Training with checkpoints in S3
Increase the number of on-demand training instances
Purchase a 3-year SageMaker Savings Plan
Use only on-demand ml.p3 instances

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Managed Spot Training uses spare capacity at a big discount, and checkpoints in S3 let interrupted jobs resume.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More on-demand: more cost.
• Savings Plan: commitment, smaller savings for this case.
• On-demand p3: full price.

Key takeaway: fault-tolerant training → Spot + checkpoints.

stem: What is the primary trade-off a team accepts when choosing Amazon EC2 Spot Instances, via SageMaker Managed Spot Training, over On-Demand Instances for a training job?

choices.text: Big savings, but capacity can be reclaimed
Higher availability SLAs than On-Demand at the same cost
Guaranteed unlimited capacity in exchange for higher cost
Spot Instances cannot be used with SageMaker at all

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Spot provides large savings, but capacity can be reclaimed with short notice.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Higher SLA: no.
• Unlimited capacity: no.
• Not usable with SageMaker: it is.

Key takeaway: Spot = discount with interruption risk.

stem: A web application uses API Gateway and AWS Lambda for its backend and needs to call a deployed SageMaker real-time endpoint to get predictions for each user request. What is the standard integration pattern?

choices.text: Lambda calls InvokeEndpoint and returns the result
Lambda reimplements the model in Python for each request
API Gateway calls the training API to retrain per request
API Gateway serves the model directly with no backend

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The Lambda function calls InvokeEndpoint through the SageMaker runtime and returns the prediction through API Gateway.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reimplement model: no.
• Retrain per request: no.
• API Gateway serves model: no.

Key takeaway: apps call endpoints via InvokeEndpoint.

stem: A team manages a SageMaker endpoint through an AWS CDK stack. They need the endpoint to update in place to a new EndpointConfig whenever the model artifact changes, without CDK deleting and recreating the endpoint, which would cause downtime. Which CDK and CloudFormation behavior should they rely on?

choices.text: Delete and redeploy the stack from scratch on every model change
Store the model artifact only in the CDK app's source code
Update EndpointConfig so the Endpoint updates in place
Disable rollback on the CloudFormation stack

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Creating a new EndpointConfig with the new model and updating the Endpoint resource to reference it updates the endpoint in place without downtime.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Redeploy stack each time: disruptive.
• Artifact in source: bad practice.
• Disable rollback: unsafe.

Key takeaway: endpoint updates → new EndpointConfig.

stem: An ML team wants a release flow: a commit triggers container build and tests, then a model pipeline run, then manual approval, then deployment. Which service ties the stages together?

choices.text: AWS CodePipeline orchestrating the stages
SageMaker Model Registry with approval events on its own
AWS CodeBuild on its own
SageMaker Feature Store

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodePipeline orchestrates stages such as source, build (CodeBuild), SageMaker pipeline execution, manual approval, and deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Registry: stores models and approvals; it doesn't orchestrate.
• CodeBuild alone: runs builds, not a multi-stage release.
• Feature Store: features.

Key takeaway: multi-stage release orchestration → CodePipeline.

stem: A pipeline must build the inference Docker image, run unit tests, and push to ECR on each commit, without managing build servers. Which service does this step?

choices.text: AWS CodeDeploy
AWS CodeBuild
AWS Config
AWS CodeArtifact

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeBuild runs builds and tests in managed containers, including docker build and push to ECR.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeDeploy: deploys revisions.
• CodeArtifact: package repository.
• Config: compliance.

Key takeaway: build and test → CodeBuild.

stem: A model-serving service on ECS needs blue/green releases with 10% canary traffic and automatic rollback on alarms. Which service performs the deployment?

choices.text: Amazon ECR
AWS CodeBuild with a deploy phase
AWS CodeCommit
AWS CodeDeploy (ECS blue/green)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeDeploy supports ECS blue/green with canary or linear traffic shifting and alarm-based rollback.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeBuild: builds.
• CodeCommit: source control.
• ECR: image storage.

Key takeaway: traffic-shifted releases → CodeDeploy.

stem: An ML team releases models quarterly with a formal stabilization period and hotfixes, while another team deploys continuously. Which branching models fit each?

choices.text: Gitflow for both, since it supports pull requests
GitHub Flow for quarterly releases; Gitflow for continuous
No branching; commit directly to main for both
Gitflow for quarterly releases; GitHub Flow for continuous

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gitflow's develop, release, and hotfix branches fit scheduled releases with stabilization. GitHub Flow's short-lived branches merged to main fit continuous delivery.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Swapped: mismatches each cadence.
• Gitflow for both: heavy for continuous delivery.
• No branching: no review or isolation.

Key takeaway: match branching to release cadence.

stem: A team wants a new SageMaker Pipeline execution to start automatically whenever a new batch of labeled training data is uploaded to a specific Amazon S3 prefix, without any manual intervention. Which combination of services achieves this?

choices.text: A notebook that a person runs manually each time data arrives
EventBridge on S3 object-created starting the pipeline
A billing alarm that starts the pipeline when spend exceeds a threshold
An IAM policy that starts pipelines whenever S3 permissions change

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule on S3 object-created events starts the SageMaker pipeline automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual notebook: not automatic.
• Billing alarm: unrelated.
• IAM policy starts pipelines: no.

Key takeaway: data arrival triggers → EventBridge.

stem: A team wants its ML steps (processing, training, evaluation, conditional registration) defined as code, rerun reproducibly, with cached steps and lineage. Which service fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Studio notebooks run by hand
SageMaker Pipelines
SageMaker Ground Truth
SageMaker Feature Store

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Pipelines defines ML workflows as a DAG of steps with conditions, step caching, parameters, and lineage tracking.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Ground Truth: labeling.
• Feature Store: features.
• Manual notebooks: not reproducible pipelines.

Key takeaway: ML workflow orchestration → SageMaker Pipelines.

stem: In an ML CI/CD pipeline, which statement correctly distinguishes a unit test from an integration test?

choices.text: Unit and integration tests are the same, just run at different stages
Unit tests need a deployed endpoint; integration tests never do
Unit tests are only for infrastructure code; integration only for model code
Unit tests one component; integration checks components together

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Unit tests check one component in isolation. Integration tests check that components work together.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same tests: no.
• Unit needs endpoint: no.
• Infrastructure only: no.

Key takeaway: unit = isolated; integration = combined.

stem: A SageMaker Pipelines CI/CD workflow passes its unit tests but consistently fails at the integration test stage, where a test invokes the newly deployed staging endpoint with sample records and compares the predictions to expected values. The failure message indicates a schema mismatch in the input features. What is the most likely root cause?

choices.text: Training and test-input preprocessing don't match
The CodePipeline role lacks permission to call CodeBuild
The training instance type was too small for the dataset
The endpoint's auto scaling policy is misconfigured

explanation:
Why this is correct:
If unit tests pass but integration fails, a common cause is training and inference preprocessing not matching, so the model receives unexpected inputs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CodeBuild permission: fails earlier.
• Small training instance: not an integration mismatch.
• Auto scaling: unrelated.

Key takeaway: keep preprocessing consistent between training and inference.

stem: A team wants to automatically retrain a production model on a regular weekly schedule, and also trigger an out-of-cycle retraining whenever SageMaker Model Monitor detects significant data drift. Which combination of services best supports both triggers?

choices.text: A single CloudFormation template that can run only once
A weekly EventBridge schedule plus a drift-alarm rule
An IAM policy that retrains models whenever any user signs in
Start the pipeline manually from Studio every week

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A weekly EventBridge schedule starts routine retraining, and a separate rule triggered by a drift alarm starts it on demand.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One-time template: no.
• IAM triggers: no.
• Manual weekly: toil.

Key takeaway: scheduled + event-driven retraining.

stem: Auditors ask which Git commit, dataset version, and pipeline run produced the model in production. Which practice fits BEST?

choices.text: Keep all models under one S3 key that is overwritten
Tag the model package with commit and run IDs
Skip version control because SageMaker tracks everything
Track this information in a shared spreadsheet

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Adding commit hash, data version, and pipeline execution ID as metadata or tags on the registered model package (plus lineage tracking) connects each deployed model to its sources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Overwritten key: destroys history.
• Nothing to configure: lineage still needs these identifiers recorded.
• Spreadsheet: disconnected and error-prone.

Key takeaway: traceability = IDs attached to the model version.

stem: A demand model's accuracy drops slowly after a new competitor enters the market, though the input feature distributions look unchanged. What kind of drift is this, and how is it detected?

choices.text: Data drift; detected by input distribution checks
Latency drift; fixed by adding endpoint instances
Concept drift; monitor model quality against labels
Hardware drift; fixed by changing instance types

explanation:
Why this is correct:
When the relationship between features and target changes while inputs look the same, that's concept drift. It shows up in model quality metrics once ground truth labels arrive.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data drift: input distributions change, which isn't the case here.
• Hardware or latency: unrelated to accuracy.

Key takeaway: inputs same, outcomes different → concept drift → model quality monitoring.

stem: A team wants to automatically detect when the statistical distribution of input features sent to a real-time SageMaker endpoint diverges significantly from the training data baseline, and raise a CloudWatch alarm when this happens. Which capability should they use?

choices.text: Model Monitor data quality monitoring
SageMaker Autopilot
SageMaker Ground Truth
SageMaker Debugger

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model Monitor data quality monitoring compares live input feature distributions with a baseline and reports drift.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Autopilot: AutoML.
• Ground Truth: labeling.
• Debugger: training.

Key takeaway: input drift → data quality monitoring.

stem: A team enabled SageMaker Model Monitor Model Quality monitoring on a real-time endpoint, but scheduled monitoring executions consistently report insufficient data to compute quality metrics such as accuracy, even though data capture is confirmed to be working. What is the most likely missing piece?

choices.text: CloudWatch Logs retention is configured too short
The endpoint instance type is too small to serve requests
The monitoring schedule uses an invalid cron expression
Ground truth labels aren't being merged

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model quality monitoring needs ground truth labels merged with captured predictions. Without labels, jobs can't compute metrics.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Log retention: unrelated.
• Instance size: unrelated.
• Invalid cron: jobs wouldn't be scheduled.

Key takeaway: model quality needs ground truth.

stem: An ML engineer must choose between SageMaker Model Monitor Data Quality monitoring and Model Quality monitoring for a use case where ground truth labels arrive three weeks after inference. Which statement correctly compares the two monitor types?

choices.text: Data quality runs on inputs now; model quality needs labels
Model quality runs immediately, while data quality waits for labels
Both monitor types require ground truth labels before any metric
Neither can be scheduled; both require manual invocation each time

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data quality monitoring runs on inputs immediately. Model quality monitoring needs ground truth labels, which often arrive later.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reversed: incorrect.
• Both need labels: only model quality.
• Can't be scheduled: both can.

Key takeaway: inputs now; accuracy later.

stem: The team wants an alarm when p99 latency of a SageMaker endpoint exceeds 500 ms for 5 minutes, and another when invocation errors spike above normal patterns. Which fits?

choices.text: CloudWatch alarms, including an anomaly detection alarm
Amazon Macie findings
AWS Config rules on the endpoint
Trusted Advisor performance checks on the endpoint

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker publishes endpoint metrics such as ModelLatency and Invocation5XXErrors to CloudWatch. Static alarms handle known thresholds, and anomaly detection alarms catch unusual spikes.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: configuration compliance.
• Trusted Advisor: best-practice checks.
• Macie: sensitive data.

Key takeaway: endpoint alerts → CloudWatch alarms.

stem: A team wants CloudWatch to automatically learn the normal seasonal pattern of an endpoint's InvocationsPerInstance metric and alert only when the metric falls far outside its expected range, without manually setting a static threshold. Which CloudWatch feature should they use?

choices.text: CloudWatch Logs Insights queries
A standard CloudWatch alarm with a fixed static threshold
CloudWatch Contributor Insights
CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms learn seasonal patterns and alert on deviations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Logs Insights: queries.
• Static threshold: no seasonality.
• Contributor Insights: top contributors.

Key takeaway: seasonal metrics → anomaly detection.

stem: A credit-scoring model is deployed to a SageMaker endpoint. The team wants to detect if the distribution of a sensitive feature, such as applicant age group, used at inference time has shifted meaningfully from the training data distribution in a way that could introduce bias drift. Which capability directly addresses this?

choices.text: Glue DataBrew data quality rules
The Model Registry approval workflow
SageMaker Neo model compilation
Clarify bias drift with Model Monitor

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clarify bias drift monitoring with Model Monitor detects when bias metrics in production predictions shift over time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DataBrew rules: data preparation.
• Registry approval: deployment.
• Neo: compilation.

Key takeaway: production bias changes → bias drift monitoring.

stem: Which statement best distinguishes SageMaker Clarify feature attribution drift monitoring from SageMaker Model Monitor data quality drift monitoring?

choices.text: Attribution drift tracks feature influence (SHAP); data drift tracks values
They are the same capability marketed under two different names
Data drift needs ground truth, while attribution drift needs no inference data
Attribution drift monitoring applies only to linear regression models

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Feature attribution drift tracks changes in feature influence (SHAP values). Data drift tracks changes in input distributions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Same capability: no.
• Ground truth reversed: neither requires it this way.
• Linear only: no.

Key takeaway: attribution drift ≠ data drift.

stem: A team wants to compare a challenger model with production on 10% of live traffic, measuring business outcomes before switching. Which setup fits?

choices.text: Two production variants weighted 90/10
Batch Transform on last month's data
Shadow variant with no responses returned
A second endpoint that clients choose randomly

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An endpoint can host multiple production variants with weights. Real users receive challenger predictions for 10% of traffic, so business outcomes can be compared.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shadow: responses aren't served, so business outcomes can't be measured.
• Offline batch: no live outcomes.
• Client-side random choice: unmanaged and inconsistent.

Key takeaway: measure live impact → weighted production variants.

stem: A team is deciding between shadow testing, where a challenger model is invoked on live traffic but its predictions are never returned to users, and A and B testing with a multi-variant endpoint, to validate a new fraud-detection model. Which factor most strongly favors shadow testing over A and B testing in this scenario?

choices.text: Shadow testing computes statistical significance faster than A/B testing
Shadow testing retrains the champion using the challenger's outputs
Evaluate on real traffic with no customer impact
The team wants to measure the challenger's effect on business KPIs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shadow testing sends copies of real traffic to the challenger without returning its responses, so it's evaluated on real data with no customer impact.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Faster significance: not the point.
• Retrains champion: no.
• Measures business effect: that needs A/B testing.

Key takeaway: safe real-traffic evaluation → shadow testing.

stem: Data quality monitoring for an endpoint reports violations on every run, including for normal traffic. The baseline was created from a small, unrepresentative sample. What should be done?

choices.text: Re-baseline from representative training data
Disable monitoring until the model is retrained
Delete all constraints so no violations appear
Raise the monitoring schedule to every minute

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model Monitor compares captured data to baseline statistics and constraints. A baseline from representative training data (and reviewed constraints) makes violations meaningful.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable monitoring: loses protection.
• More frequent runs: more noise.
• Deleting constraints: removes detection entirely.

Key takeaway: good monitoring starts with a representative baseline.

stem: A team enabled SageMaker Model Monitor on a real-time endpoint, but the scheduled monitoring executions consistently fail with an error indicating no captured data was found at the specified Amazon S3 location. What is the most likely cause?

choices.text: The training job that produced the model used an incorrect IAM role
Data capture isn't enabled in the endpoint config
The monitoring schedule's cron expression is invalid
The model artifact was never registered in the Model Registry

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model Monitor needs data capture enabled in the endpoint configuration. Without captured data, monitoring jobs have nothing to analyze.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Training IAM: unrelated.
• Invalid cron: wouldn't schedule.
• Registry: unrelated.

Key takeaway: monitoring needs data capture.

stem: An ML engineer orchestrates a multi-step SageMaker Pipeline for daily batch scoring and wants to be notified automatically whenever any pipeline step fails or the overall execution status changes. Which combination of services best achieves this?

choices.text: AWS Trusted Advisor checks on the pipeline
Cost Explorer anomaly detection for failed runs
Amazon Macie sensitive data alerts
EventBridge on pipeline status changes, to SNS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
An EventBridge rule on pipeline execution status changes (such as Failed) routes to SNS for notifications.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Trusted Advisor: no.
• Cost anomaly: no.
• Macie: no.

Key takeaway: pipeline alerts → EventBridge + SNS.

stem: After enabling data quality monitoring, a team sees violation reports flagging extra column and missing column checks on every scheduled run, even though the model continues to return valid-looking predictions. What most likely explains these specific violations?

choices.text: Captured data's schema doesn't match the baseline
A Logs Insights query used by the monitor has a syntax error
The model's execution role lacks permission to read from S3
The endpoint is under-provisioned and drops some requests

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Extra-column and type violations mean the captured data's schema doesn't match the baseline, often due to a changed request format.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Logs Insights syntax: not used.
• S3 permission: jobs would fail.
• Under-provisioned endpoint: unrelated.

Key takeaway: schema violations → input format changed.

stem: A clinical model must be checked continuously for growing disparity in positive predictions between demographic groups, with alerts. Which approach fits?

choices.text: SageMaker JumpStart model evaluation run monthly
Feature Store online store queries
Clarify bias drift monitoring with Model Monitor
Ground Truth Plus labeling reviews

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clarify integrates with Model Monitor to compute bias metrics on production data over time and raise alerts when they cross thresholds.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Feature Store: storage.
• JumpStart: pretrained models.
• Ground Truth Plus: labeling.

Key takeaway: bias over time in production → bias drift monitoring.

stem: An endpoint's clients report slowness. Which set of CloudWatch metrics best separates model compute time from SageMaker overhead and shows whether instances are saturated?

choices.text: Invocations and TrainingJobStatus
ModelLatency, OverheadLatency, utilization
NumberOfHumanWorkersActivated
S3 bucket size of the model artifacts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ModelLatency measures time in the container, OverheadLatency measures SageMaker overhead, and utilization shows saturation. Together they locate the bottleneck.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Invocations and training status: volume and training, not latency breakdown.
• Human workers: labeling.
• Artifact size: unrelated to runtime latency.

Key takeaway: split latency into model vs. overhead, and check utilization.

stem: An SRE wants a way to express the percentage of successful invocations versus total invocations for a SageMaker endpoint over the last hour, to track availability. Which pair of metrics should be combined?

choices.text: CPUUtilization and MemoryUtilization
Invocations and Invocation5XXErrors (1 − error ratio)
ModelLatency and OverheadLatency only
GPUUtilization and DiskUtilization

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Availability can be expressed as 1 minus (Invocation5XXErrors ÷ Invocations).

Why the other options are wrong:
• CPU and memory: resource use.
• Latency only: not success rate.
• GPU and disk: resource use.

Key takeaway: success rate from invocation and error metrics.

stem: A Lambda function that pre-processes features before invoking a SageMaker endpoint is intermittently timing out. The team wants a fast way to see the function's memory usage, cold start counts, and CPU usage without writing custom metrics code. Which tool should they enable?

choices.text: AWS Config rules
SageMaker Debugger
AWS Trusted Advisor
CloudWatch Lambda Insights

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch Lambda Insights provides detailed function performance metrics, such as memory, CPU, and duration, to diagnose intermittent slowness.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: configuration.
• Debugger: training.
• Trusted Advisor: best practices.

Key takeaway: Lambda performance diagnosis → Lambda Insights.

stem: An ML engineer needs to quickly query several days of SageMaker endpoint invocation logs to find the specific requests that produced the highest ModelLatency values, without standing up a separate analytics pipeline. Which service should they use?

choices.text: Amazon Athena queries against CloudTrail logs
The AWS X-Ray service map
CloudWatch Logs Insights
Amazon QuickSight

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudWatch Logs Insights queries days of log data quickly with filters and aggregations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Athena on CloudTrail: API calls.
• X-Ray map: traces.
• QuickSight: BI.

Key takeaway: ad hoc log queries → Logs Insights.

stem: A security review must show who deleted a SageMaker endpoint last month and from which IP. Which source fits?

choices.text: CloudWatch endpoint metrics for Invocations
AWS Config conformance pack scores
AWS CloudTrail event history or trail logs
SageMaker Model Monitor reports

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CloudTrail records SageMaker API calls such as DeleteEndpoint, with the principal, time, and source IP.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Metrics: performance, not who did what.
• Model Monitor: data and model quality.
• Conformance scores: compliance status.

Key takeaway: who called which API → CloudTrail.

stem: A team is choosing an instance type for a real-time SageMaker endpoint serving a deep learning image classification model that benefits heavily from GPU acceleration, while also needing to control costs for bursty, unpredictable traffic. Which choice best balances performance and cost?

choices.text: The largest CPU-only instance permanently, to avoid any GPU cost
GPU instances with endpoint auto scaling
A real-time endpoint on Spot Instances
Serverless Inference regardless of the GPU acceleration requirement

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A GPU-accelerated model needs GPU instances, and endpoint auto scaling adjusts instance count to demand.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CPU permanently: too slow.
• Spot for real-time endpoints: not supported.
• Serverless: no GPU.

Key takeaway: GPU inference with variable load → GPU + auto scaling.

stem: Finance wants a list of SageMaker endpoints and EC2 instances that are idle or underutilized across accounts, as a starting point for savings. Which tool fits?

choices.text: Trusted Advisor cost checks (org view)
AWS Config conformance packs for cost rules
AWS CloudTrail Lake queries
Amazon Macie findings

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks flag idle or underutilized resources, including SageMaker endpoints and EC2 instances, and organizational view aggregates across accounts. Compute Optimizer adds deeper rightsizing.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Config: compliance.
• CloudTrail Lake: API activity.
• Macie: sensitive data.

Key takeaway: idle resources → Trusted Advisor.

stem: A ML platform team wants to break down and visualize monthly SageMaker costs by individual project team, using cost allocation tags applied to training jobs and endpoints. Which service should they use to analyze this cost data over time?

choices.text: SageMaker Model Registry
Amazon CloudWatch metrics
Cost Explorer with cost allocation tags
AWS X-Ray

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cost Explorer with activated cost allocation tags (such as project) breaks down SageMaker costs by project.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Model Registry: models.
• CloudWatch: metrics.
• X-Ray: traces.

Key takeaway: cost by project → tags + Cost Explorer.

stem: The ML platform must split SageMaker costs by project and environment, and restrict users to resources of their own project. Which practice supports both?

choices.text: Separate IAM users per project with no tags
Consistent tags: cost allocation and ABAC conditions
Enabling Model Monitor on every endpoint for usage reports
Encrypting resources with project-specific keys

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Activated cost allocation tags break down costs, and IAM conditions on resource and principal tags restrict access by project.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Users without tags: no cost breakdown.
• Per-project keys: encryption, not cost or access by tag.
• Model Monitor: unrelated.

Key takeaway: tags drive both cost allocation and ABAC.

stem: Before deploying a new model to production, a team wants an automated, data-driven recommendation for the most cost-effective instance type and endpoint configuration that meets a specific latency SLA, based on load testing against their actual model artifact. Which SageMaker feature should they use?

choices.text: SageMaker Clarify
SageMaker Ground Truth
SageMaker Data Wrangler
SageMaker Inference Recommender

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Inference Recommender load-tests the model on instance types and recommends the best cost and performance option.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Clarify: bias.
• Ground Truth: labeling.
• Data Wrangler: preparation.

Key takeaway: choose endpoint instances → Inference Recommender.

stem: How does SageMaker Inference Recommender differ from AWS Compute Optimizer when it comes to right-sizing ML infrastructure?

choices.text: Recommender load-tests before deployment; Compute Optimizer analyzes running usage
Compute Optimizer can analyze only SageMaker endpoints, not EC2 instances
They are the same service offered under different names in different Regions
Recommender works only after a model has run in production for 30 days

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inference Recommender load-tests before deployment. Compute Optimizer analyzes historical utilization of running resources.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Compute Optimizer only SageMaker: no.
• Same service: no.
• Recommender only after production: no.

Key takeaway: pre-deployment testing vs. post-deployment analysis.

stem: A team runs large, fault-tolerant SageMaker training jobs frequently but at unpredictable times, and separately maintains a steady-state, always-on real-time inference endpoint. Which combination of purchasing options is most cost-effective?

choices.text: Reserved Instances for training and On-Demand for the endpoint
On-Demand for both, since SageMaker supports neither Spot nor Savings Plans
Spot training with checkpoints; a Savings Plan for the endpoint
Spot Instances for the always-on endpoint and On-Demand for training

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Spot training with checkpoints saves on fault-tolerant training, and a Savings Plan discounts the always-on endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• RIs for training: not how SageMaker is priced.
• On-Demand for both: no savings.
• Spot for endpoint: not supported.

Key takeaway: match pricing to each workload pattern.

stem: A training job fails with AccessDenied reading its training data in S3 and pulling a custom image from ECR, although the data scientist who launched it has access. Why?

choices.text: SageMaker uses root credentials, which are blocked
The job's execution role lacks S3 and ECR permissions
The training instance type can't reach S3 without a larger network size
The data scientist's IAM user needs more permissions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker jobs act with the execution role passed at launch (via iam:PassRole), not the caller's identity. That role needs S3 read and ECR pull permissions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Caller permissions: the job doesn't use them for data access.
• Root credentials: not used.
• Instance type: unrelated to authorization.

Key takeaway: jobs use their execution role.

stem: A platform team onboarding many data scientists to SageMaker Studio wants a guided way to create IAM roles with appropriately scoped permissions for common ML personas, such as data scientist or MLOps engineer, without hand-writing policy JSON from scratch. Which feature should they use?

choices.text: AWS IAM Access Analyzer
AWS Organizations service control policies
Amazon SageMaker Role Manager
Amazon Cognito user pools

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Role Manager provides guided creation of least-privilege roles for ML personas.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Access Analyzer: analysis.
• SCPs: guardrails.
• Cognito: app users.

Key takeaway: ML persona roles → Role Manager.

stem: A team attaches an S3 read policy to an IAM group and also wants SageMaker jobs to read the same bucket. Which statement is correct?

choices.text: Roles are permission documents; policies are assumable identities
Policies can be attached only to roles, never to groups
Policies grant permissions; SageMaker assumes a role
The group's policy automatically applies to SageMaker jobs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Policies are documents listing permissions and attach to users, groups, or roles. SageMaker jobs assume an execution role, so the permissions must be on that role.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reversed definitions: incorrect.
• Group policy applying to jobs: jobs don't act as group members.
• Policies only on roles: they attach to groups too.

Key takeaway: permissions live in policies; services act through roles.

stem: A healthcare company must ensure that data stored in a SageMaker Feature Store and all training job output artifacts are encrypted at rest using a customer-managed key they control, rather than an AWS-managed default key. Which service or feature should they configure?

choices.text: Secrets Manager automatic key rotation
KMS customer managed keys in SageMaker configs
AWS Certificate Manager
Amazon Macie automatic encryption

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Specifying KMS customer managed keys in Feature Store, training, and model configurations encrypts data and artifacts with company-controlled keys.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Secrets Manager rotation: secrets.
• ACM: certificates.
• Macie encryption: Macie doesn't encrypt.

Key takeaway: customer-controlled encryption → CMKs in SageMaker configs.

stem: A financial services company requires that all traffic between a SageMaker Studio notebook and the SageMaker training and inference APIs stay entirely within their VPC and never traverse the public internet. Which approach satisfies this requirement?

choices.text: Allow the SageMaker API's public IP ranges in a security group
VPC mode plus PrivateLink endpoints for SageMaker
Route all SageMaker API traffic through a NAT gateway
Enable Amazon S3 Transfer Acceleration

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Running Studio in VPC-only mode with PrivateLink interface endpoints for SageMaker APIs keeps traffic off the public internet.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Allow public IPs: still internet.
• NAT gateway: still internet.
• Transfer Acceleration: unrelated.

Key takeaway: private SageMaker access → VPC mode + endpoints.

stem: A training job in a VPC must reach only an internal feature API on port 443 and S3 via a gateway endpoint. Which control restricts the job's network traffic at the ENI level?

choices.text: A KMS key policy on the output key
A SageMaker lifecycle configuration
A security group on the job's ENIs
An IAM policy on the execution role

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Security groups are stateful firewalls on the network interfaces SageMaker creates in your subnets, restricting outbound and inbound traffic.

Why the other options are wrong:
• IAM: authorizes API calls, not network traffic.
• KMS: encryption access.
• Lifecycle configuration: notebook setup scripts.

Key takeaway: network paths → security groups; API permissions → IAM.

stem: An ML engineer must ensure a SageMaker training job that processes highly sensitive data cannot make any outbound network calls to the internet, even accidentally through a compromised dependency. Which configuration option should be enabled on the training job?

choices.text: Enable network isolation on the training job
Disable data capture on the training job
Run the job in a public subnet with an auto-assigned public IP
Attach an internet gateway to the training subnet

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Network isolation on the training job blocks all inbound and outbound network access from the container.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable data capture: endpoints only.
• Public subnet: opposite.
• Internet gateway: opposite.

Key takeaway: no network for training → network isolation.

stem: An MLOps pipeline builds images and deploys models across dev and prod accounts. Security bans long-term keys in pipelines. Which practice fits?

choices.text: One shared access key for every pipeline stage
Disabling IAM checks for the pipeline
An IAM user's access keys in the buildspec
Service roles assuming scoped cross-account roles

explanation:
Why this is correct:
CodeBuild and CodePipeline run with service roles that get temporary credentials and can assume narrowly scoped roles in other accounts for deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keys in buildspec: long-term secrets in code.
• Shared key: long-term and over-privileged.
• Disabling IAM: not possible or safe.

Key takeaway: pipelines use roles, not keys.

stem: A security review finds that a CI/CD pipeline deploying ML models pulls container images from a public, unauthenticated registry and pushes them directly to a SageMaker endpoint with no verification step. What is the best mitigation to reduce the risk of a compromised or tampered image being deployed?

choices.text: Disable CloudTrail logging on the pipeline account to simplify audits
Keep pulling from the public registry, but only during off-peak hours
Increase the endpoint's instance count to limit a bad deployment's impact
A scanned private ECR repo plus a verification stage

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Pull images from a private, scanned ECR repository and add a pipeline stage that verifies images before deployment.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable CloudTrail: worse.
• Off-peak public pulls: still risky.
• More instances: unrelated.

Key takeaway: supply chain security → private scanned images + verification.

stem: A company wants only a small, designated group of ML engineers to be able to approve a model version in SageMaker Model Registry for production deployment, while data scientists can register new model versions but not approve them. How should this be implemented?

choices.text: Give everyone the same admin role and rely on team communication
Disable versioning in the Model Registry to prevent unauthorized changes
IAM lets scientists register; only ML engineers can approve
Track approval decisions in a shared spreadsheet outside AWS

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IAM policies let data scientists register model versions while only ML engineers can update approval status.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shared admin role: no control.
• Disable versioning: breaks the registry.
• Spreadsheet: no enforcement.

Key takeaway: approval control → IAM on Model Registry actions.

stem: A security team wants to be automatically alerted if an IAM principal that has never called SageMaker APIs before suddenly starts calling CreateTrainingJob and CreateEndpoint many times in a short window, which could indicate compromised credentials. Which AWS service is designed to detect this kind of anomalous behavioral pattern?

choices.text: AWS Budgets
Amazon Rekognition
Amazon GuardDuty
AWS Trusted Advisor

explanation:
Why this is correct:
GuardDuty detects anomalous API behavior, such as a principal suddenly calling SageMaker APIs it never used.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Budgets: spend.
• Rekognition: images.
• Trusted Advisor: best practices.

Key takeaway: anomalous API use → GuardDuty.

stem: A fraud dataset has 0.4% positive labels. A model reports 99.6% accuracy but catches almost no fraud. Which TWO actions are MOST appropriate? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Remove all positive examples to simplify training.
Apply SMOTE to the full dataset before the train/test split.
Use precision, recall, and PR-AUC.
Keep accuracy as the primary metric because it is already high.
Class weights or resampling on the training split only.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Use precision, recall, and PR-AUC to evaluate the rare class, and apply class weights or resampling to the training split only.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove positives: nonsense.
• SMOTE before split: leaks synthetic data into test.
• Keep accuracy: misleading.

Key takeaway: imbalance → right metrics + train-only resampling.

stem: A recommendation model needs the same customer features during training on historical data and at inference time with single-digit millisecond lookups. The team wants to avoid training-serving skew. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: Store features in CSV files in S3 and read them in the endpoint.
Recompute features in the inference container from raw logs per request.
Feature Store: online for inference, offline for training.
Keep features only in a Redshift table queried at inference.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Feature Store provides the online store for low-latency inference lookups and the offline store for training, keeping features consistent.

Why the other options are wrong:
• CSV in S3 for inference: slow.
• Recompute in container: inconsistent.
• Redshift at inference: slow.

Key takeaway: training/serving consistency → Feature Store.

stem: A model scores 0.97 AUC in validation but 0.71 in production. Investigation shows the team standardized features using the mean and standard deviation of the entire dataset before splitting. What is the problem and fix?

choices.text: Underfitting; add more layers to the model.
Concept drift; retrain the model daily.
Leakage; fit the scaler on training data only.
Class imbalance; oversample the minority class.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fitting the scaler on the full dataset leaks information from validation data. Fit it on training data only.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Underfitting: not indicated.
• Concept drift: the gap comes from leakage.
• Class imbalance: unrelated.

Key takeaway: fit preprocessing on training data only.

stem: Before training a credit model, the team must check whether the training data is imbalanced across an age group facet and whether positive labels are distributed differently between groups. Which tool and metrics fit BEST?

choices.text: SageMaker Debugger vanishing gradient rules.
Amazon Macie sensitive data discovery.
Clarify pre-training bias metrics (CI, DPL).
Model Monitor model quality metrics.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clarify pre-training bias metrics such as CI and DPL check imbalance across groups in training data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Debugger: training dynamics.
• Macie: sensitive data.
• Model quality: predictions.

Key takeaway: data bias before training → Clarify pre-training metrics.

stem: A feature contains 40,000 distinct ZIP codes. One-hot encoding creates a very sparse, huge feature matrix that slows training. Which approach is MOST appropriate for a tree-based model?

choices.text: Target-encode (fold-fitted) or group into regions.
Drop the feature, since high-cardinality features never help.
Label-encode ZIPs as integers and treat them as continuous.
Duplicate the one-hot columns to increase signal.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Target encoding fitted within folds, or grouping ZIPs into regions, captures signal without a huge sparse matrix.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Drop the feature: may lose signal.
• Label encode as continuous: false order.
• Duplicate columns: no.

Key takeaway: high cardinality → target encoding or grouping.

stem: Training accuracy is 99% while validation accuracy is 72% and falls as training continues. Which TWO actions are MOST likely to help? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Use early stopping based on validation loss.
Train for more epochs.
Increase model depth substantially.
Add regularization such as L2 or dropout.
Remove the validation set to use more training data for the report.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Early stopping on validation loss and regularization such as L2 or dropout reduce overfitting.

Why the other options are wrong:
• More epochs: worse.
• More depth: worse.
• Remove validation: loses monitoring.

Key takeaway: overfitting → early stopping + regularization.

stem: A team must tune eight hyperparameters of an expensive model with a budget of about 60 training jobs. Which tuning configuration is MOST efficient?

choices.text: Grid search over all combinations.
Manual tuning of one parameter at a time.
Bayesian search with early stopping.
Random search with 5 jobs.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bayesian search picks promising combinations from earlier results, and early stopping ends poor jobs, fitting a 60-job budget.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Grid search: too many combinations.
• Manual one at a time: inefficient.
• Random with 5 jobs: too few.

Key takeaway: limited tuning budget → Bayesian + early stopping.

stem: A 30-billion-parameter model does not fit into the memory of a single GPU, even with batch size 1. Which training approach is required?

choices.text: Data parallelism across more instances.
Model parallelism or fully sharded data parallelism.
Increasing the instance's EBS volume size.
Using a larger learning rate.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model parallelism or fully sharded data parallelism splits the model's parameters across GPUs so it fits in memory.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data parallelism: each GPU holds the full model.
• EBS size: not GPU memory.
• Learning rate: unrelated.

Key takeaway: model too large for one GPU → model parallel / FSDP.

stem: Training jobs run for 20 hours on GPU instances, and cost must be cut significantly. Jobs can tolerate interruption if progress is not lost. What should the team do?

choices.text: Run the jobs in a SageMaker notebook instance.
Managed spot training with S3 checkpoints.
Disable checkpointing to reduce I/O.
On-demand instances with larger batch sizes.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Managed Spot Training with S3 checkpoints cuts GPU cost substantially while resuming after interruptions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Notebook instance: not for training jobs.
• Disable checkpointing: loses progress.
• On-demand larger batches: still full price.

Key takeaway: long interruptible training → Spot + checkpoints.

stem: A delivery-time model is evaluated for a business where large errors (late by hours) are far more costly than many small errors. Which evaluation metric best reflects this preference?

choices.text: Mean absolute error (MAE).
Root mean squared error (RMSE).
Accuracy.
F1 score.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RMSE squares errors before averaging, penalizing large errors more heavily than MAE.

Why the other options are wrong:
• MAE: treats errors linearly.
• Accuracy and F1: classification metrics.

Key takeaway: penalize large errors → RMSE.

stem: Regulators ask why a loan model denied individual applicants, and the team needs per-prediction feature attributions. Which approach fits BEST?

choices.text: A confusion matrix of the validation set.
Clarify SHAP explanations per prediction.
CloudWatch invocation metrics for the endpoint.
Model Monitor data quality reports.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clarify SHAP explanations provide per-prediction feature attributions explaining individual decisions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Confusion matrix: aggregate.
• Invocation metrics: operational.
• Data quality reports: drift.

Key takeaway: per-decision explanations → SHAP via Clarify.

stem: An internal model receives a few hundred requests per day in unpredictable bursts with long idle periods. Occasional cold-start latency is acceptable, and the team wants to pay nothing while idle. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: A multi-model endpoint on large instances.
Batch Transform every minute.
SageMaker Serverless Inference.
A real-time endpoint on a GPU instance.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Serverless Inference scales to zero during idle periods and handles bursts, paying only for usage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Multi-model on large instances: idle cost.
• Batch every minute: not real-time.
• GPU real-time: idle cost.

Key takeaway: sporadic traffic → Serverless Inference.

stem: Users upload 800 MB medical images, and each prediction takes up to 20 minutes. Clients can poll for results, and the endpoint should scale to zero when idle. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: Lambda with the model loaded in memory.
A real-time inference endpoint.
Serverless Inference.
Asynchronous inference (S3 I/O, SNS).

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Asynchronous inference handles large payloads via S3, long processing times, and notifies via SNS so clients can poll.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Lambda: payload and time limits.
• Real-time: time and payload limits.
• Serverless: limits.

Key takeaway: large inputs + long processing → async inference.

stem: A SaaS company trains a separate small XGBoost model for each of 2,000 customers. Most models are called rarely. Hosting one endpoint per model is too expensive. Which option fits BEST?

choices.text: Merge all models into one by averaging their weights.
A multi-model endpoint loading from S3.
Batch Transform for all real-time requests.
One real-time endpoint per customer.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A multi-model endpoint loads per-customer models from S3 on demand, serving 2,000 models cheaply.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Averaging weights: breaks models.
• Batch Transform: not real-time.
• Endpoint per customer: costly.

Key takeaway: many small models → multi-model endpoint.

stem: When updating a production endpoint to a new model version, the team wants traffic shifted gradually and automatically rolled back if latency or error alarms fire. Which feature fits BEST?

choices.text: Delete the endpoint and create a new one.
Deployment guardrails with alarm rollback.
Update the model artifact in S3 in place.
Shadow testing with no traffic shifting.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker deployment guardrails shift traffic gradually (canary or linear) and roll back automatically on alarms.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete and recreate: downtime.
• Update artifact in place: no control.
• Shadow without shifting: no rollout.

Key takeaway: safe endpoint updates → deployment guardrails.

stem: A deployed model's accuracy degrades slowly because incoming feature distributions differ from training data. The team wants automated alerts when input distributions drift. What should it configure?

choices.text: Retrain the model every hour regardless of drift.
Increase the endpoint's instance count.
Data capture plus a baselined data quality monitor.
Enable CloudTrail on the endpoint.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Enabling data capture and a data quality monitor with a baseline detects feature distribution drift.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Hourly retraining: wasteful.
• More instances: unrelated.
• CloudTrail: API calls.

Key takeaway: detect drift → data capture + baselined monitor.

stem: The team must choose the most cost-effective instance type for an endpoint that must meet a p95 latency of 100 ms at 300 requests per second. Which tool fits BEST?

choices.text: Model Monitor bias reports.
Inference Recommender load tests.
AWS Pricing Calculator only.
Trusted Advisor idle resource checks.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inference Recommender load tests find the most cost-effective instance meeting the p95 latency target.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Bias reports: unrelated.
• Pricing Calculator only: no performance data.
• Idle checks: unrelated.

Key takeaway: latency-constrained instance selection → Inference Recommender.

stem: Endpoint traffic rises fivefold during business hours. The team wants instance count to follow load automatically. Which configuration is standard?

choices.text: Target tracking scaling on SageMakerVariantInvocationsPerInstance for the production variant.
Schedule a manual resize every morning.
Scale on the endpoint's disk utilization.
Increase model size to handle peak load.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Target tracking on SageMakerVariantInvocationsPerInstance adjusts instance count as load rises and falls.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manual resize: toil.
• Disk utilization: not load.
• Bigger model: no.

Key takeaway: endpoint auto scaling → invocations per instance.

stem: Security requires that training containers cannot make any outbound network calls, while still reading training data from S3 privately. Which configuration meets this?

choices.text: Use a NAT gateway with a deny-all route.
Run training jobs in a public subnet with a restrictive security group.
Encrypt the training data with KMS only.
Run training jobs in a VPC with network isolation enabled, and use an S3 gateway endpoint for data access.

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Running training jobs in a VPC with network isolation blocks outbound calls, while VPC endpoints (such as the S3 gateway endpoint) let SageMaker access data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• NAT deny-all: not a feature.
• Public subnet: opposite.
• KMS only: doesn't block network.

Key takeaway: no egress but data access → isolation + VPC endpoints.

stem: A training job reads a 2 TB dataset of many small files from S3 and spends most of its time waiting for data to download before training starts. Which input mode reduces startup time with minimal changes?

choices.text: Splitting the job into 2,000 separate training jobs
FastFile mode, which streams S3 objects on demand
File mode with a larger EBS volume on the instance
Copying the data to the notebook instance first

explanation:
Why this is correct:
FastFile mode exposes S3 data as files and streams it on demand, so training starts without a full download.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Splitting the job into 2,000 separate…: Splitting the job does not train one model.
• File mode with a larger EBS volume on the…: File mode still downloads everything first.
• Copying the data to the notebook instance first: Copying to a notebook adds a step and does not help the training job.

Key takeaway: Avoid full downloads with FastFile or Pipe mode.

stem: A distributed training job needs a high-throughput shared file system in front of an S3 dataset, with repeated epochs reading the same data. Which option fits?

choices.text: Amazon EFS One Zone with bursting throughput
Amazon FSx for Lustre linked to the S3 bucket
S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval for all training files
An EBS volume attached to only the first instance

explanation:
Why this is correct:
FSx for Lustre provides high-throughput parallel access and can be linked to S3 data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon EFS One Zone with bursting throughput: EFS is not optimized for this throughput.
• S3 Glacier Instant Retrieval for all…: Glacier is archival.
• An EBS volume attached to only the first…: An EBS volume cannot be shared by all instances.

Key takeaway: High-throughput training data → FSx for Lustre.

stem: Clickstream events must be captured continuously and stored in S3 as Parquet for later feature engineering, with no servers to manage. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon SQS standard queue with polling
Amazon Data Firehose with format conversion
AWS Snowball Edge collecting events on site
Amazon EBS snapshots of the web servers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Firehose ingests streams and converts them to Parquet in S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon SQS standard queue with polling: SQS does not deliver data to S3 by itself.
• AWS Snowball Edge collecting events on site: Snowball is for offline bulk transfer.
• Amazon EBS snapshots of the web servers: Snapshots do not capture events.

Key takeaway: Stream to S3 in Parquet with Firehose.

stem: A team needs features to be available with millisecond latency at inference time and also kept historically for training, with consistent definitions. Which service fits?

choices.text: A spreadsheet shared by the data science team
SageMaker Feature Store with online and offline stores
An ElastiCache cluster that keeps no historical feature data
A single CSV file in S3 updated once a week

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Feature Store provides a low-latency online store and an offline store for training, from shared feature definitions.

Why the other options are wrong:
