• A spreadsheet shared by the data science team: Spreadsheets do not scale.
• An ElastiCache cluster that keeps no…: A cache without history cannot support training.
• A single CSV file in S3 updated once a week: A weekly CSV is not low latency.

Key takeaway: Consistent online and offline features → Feature Store.

stem: Which file format usually reduces storage and speeds up column-wise analytics during data preparation?

choices.text: Uncompressed JSON
Apache Parquet
Plain CSV text
Raw XML files

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Parquet is columnar and compressed, which reduces storage and speeds column reads.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Uncompressed JSON: Uncompressed JSON is verbose.
• Plain CSV text: CSV is row-based and uncompressed.
• Raw XML files: XML is verbose.

Key takeaway: Columnar formats speed analytics.

stem: A tabular dataset has a numeric feature with 5% missing values that are missing at random. What is a reasonable first approach?

choices.text: Delete the entire feature because any missing value makes it unusable
Impute missing values with the median and add a missing-indicator feature
Duplicate rows that have values so the missing ones become rare
Replace missing values with a very large number such as 999,999

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Median imputation is robust, and an indicator preserves information about missingness.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Delete the entire feature because any…: Dropping a useful feature loses signal.
• Duplicate rows that have values so the…: Duplicating rows biases the data.
• Replace missing values with a very large…: Sentinel values distort distributions.

Key takeaway: Impute sensibly and keep missingness information.

stem: A categorical feature has 20,000 unique values. One-hot encoding creates a huge sparse matrix. Which approach is more practical?

choices.text: Dropping all rows that contain uncommon category values
Target encoding or learned embeddings, with safeguards against leakage
One-hot encoding with even more columns for rare categories
Label encoding treated as a continuous numeric feature in linear models

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Target encoding or embeddings represent high-cardinality categories compactly; leakage must be prevented with proper splits.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Dropping all rows that contain uncommon…: Dropping rows loses data.
• One-hot encoding with even more columns for…: More one-hot columns worsen sparsity.
• Label encoding treated as a continuous…: Label encoding implies a false order for linear models.

Key takeaway: High-cardinality categories → target encoding or embeddings.

stem: Features on very different scales (age in years, income in dollars) slow gradient-based training. Which transformation helps?

choices.text: One-hot encoding each numeric value separately
Standardization to zero mean and unit variance
Sorting the rows by income before training
Removing the feature with the larger range

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Standardizing puts features on comparable scales, helping gradient-based optimization.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One-hot encoding each numeric value separately: One-hot encoding numbers is inappropriate.
• Sorting the rows by income before training: Sorting rows does not change scales.
• Removing the feature with the larger range: Removing features loses signal.

Key takeaway: Scale features for gradient-based models.

stem: A data scientist computes normalization statistics on the full dataset before splitting into train and test sets. What is the problem?

choices.text: Overflow, because statistics cannot be computed on large data
Data leakage, because test data influenced the training transformation
Underfitting, because normalization removes useful variation
Class imbalance, because normalization changes label counts

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fitting transformations on all data leaks test information; statistics should be fit on training data only.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Overflow, because statistics cannot be…: Overflow is not the issue.
• Underfitting, because normalization removes…: Normalization does not cause underfitting by itself.
• Class imbalance, because normalization…: Normalization does not change labels.

Key takeaway: Fit preprocessing on training data only.

stem: A team wants a visual tool to explore, clean, and transform data for ML with hundreds of built-in transformations and export to a pipeline. Which tool fits?

choices.text: AWS CloudTrail Lake event data store
Amazon Inspector with custom scans
Amazon Athena with only SQL SELECT queries
SageMaker Data Wrangler (in SageMaker Canvas)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data Wrangler provides visual data preparation with built-in transforms and export to pipelines.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS CloudTrail Lake event data store: CloudTrail Lake stores API events.
• Amazon Inspector with custom scans: Inspector scans vulnerabilities.
• Amazon Athena with only SQL SELECT queries: Athena queries data but lacks ML-focused transforms and export.

Key takeaway: Visual ML data prep → Data Wrangler.

stem: A fraud dataset has 0.5% positive labels, and the model predicts everything as negative. Which TWO actions help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Remove all positive examples to simplify training
Resample, for example oversampling positives or using SMOTE
Shuffle labels randomly to balance the classes
Evaluate only with overall accuracy on the test set
Use class weights so errors on positives cost more

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Resampling and class weighting counter imbalance so the model learns the minority class.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Remove all positive examples to simplify…: Removing positives destroys the signal.
• Shuffle labels randomly to balance the classes: Shuffling labels destroys meaning.
• Evaluate only with overall accuracy on the…: Accuracy hides poor minority performance.

Key takeaway: Handle imbalance with resampling and class weights.

stem: Text reviews must be converted into numeric features for a classical classifier. Which approach is a reasonable baseline?

choices.text: One column per review with its length only
Random numbers assigned to each unique word
The review's timestamp converted to seconds
TF-IDF vectors of the tokenized text

explanation:
Why this is correct:
TF-IDF represents word importance and works well as a baseline for text classification.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One column per review with its length only: Length alone loses content.
• Random numbers assigned to each unique word: Random numbers carry no meaning.
• The review's timestamp converted to seconds: Timestamps are not text content.

Key takeaway: Baseline text features → TF-IDF.

stem: A time-series forecasting dataset is randomly shuffled before splitting into training and validation sets. Why is this a problem?

choices.text: Shuffling makes the dataset too small for the algorithm to learn
Future information leaks into training, inflating validation scores
Shuffling removes seasonality from the underlying data values
Shuffling converts the time series into a classification problem

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Time-series validation must preserve order so the model is evaluated on future data it has not seen.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Shuffling makes the dataset too small for…: Shuffling does not change size.
• Shuffling removes seasonality from the…: Values stay the same; the evaluation becomes leaky.
• Shuffling converts the time series into a…: The problem type does not change.

Key takeaway: Split time series chronologically.

stem: A company needs thousands of images labeled by human workers with automated labeling to reduce cost. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels without any labels
Amazon Comprehend custom classification only
SageMaker Ground Truth with automated data labeling
AWS Glue DataBrew recipes for image files

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Ground Truth manages human labeling workflows and can use active learning to label automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels without any…: Custom Labels needs labeled data.
• Amazon Comprehend custom classification only: Comprehend works on text.
• AWS Glue DataBrew recipes for image files: DataBrew prepares tabular data.

Key takeaway: Human labeling at scale → Ground Truth.

stem: Before training a lending model, a team must check whether the training data is imbalanced across age groups. Which tool fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Model Monitor schedules
SageMaker Debugger built-in training rules
SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias metrics
SageMaker Neo compilation jobs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clarify computes pre-training bias metrics such as class imbalance across facets.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SageMaker Model Monitor schedules: Model Monitor watches deployed models.
• SageMaker Debugger built-in training rules: Debugger inspects training.
• SageMaker Neo compilation jobs: Neo compiles models.

Key takeaway: Pre-training bias checks → Clarify.

stem: A dataset contains customer names and email addresses that must not be used for training. Which step fits?

choices.text: Encrypt the dataset so the model cannot read the PII
Detect and remove or mask PII during preprocessing
Train on the PII and delete the model after testing
Keep PII in the data and restrict the model's outputs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Removing or masking PII before training prevents it from being learned or leaked.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Encrypt the dataset so the model cannot read…: Encryption at rest does not remove PII from training.
• Train on the PII and delete the model after…: Training on PII already exposes it.
• Keep PII in the data and restrict the…: Output restrictions do not remove training exposure.

Key takeaway: Remove PII before training.

stem: A team wants automated data quality checks (completeness, uniqueness, value ranges) on training data before each pipeline run. Which option fits?

choices.text: Increasing the number of training epochs to compensate for bad data
A manual review of a random sample of rows every quarter by an analyst
Training the model first and checking data quality only if accuracy drops
AWS Glue Data Quality rules or Data Wrangler quality reports in the pipeline

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Automated quality rules catch bad data before training runs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Increasing the number of training epochs to…: More epochs cannot fix bad data.
• A manual review of a random sample of rows…: Quarterly manual checks are too slow.
• Training the model first and checking data…: Checking after training wastes resources.

Key takeaway: Gate training on automated data quality checks.

stem: Which data split is appropriate for tuning hyperparameters without biasing the final performance estimate?

choices.text: Test set only, with no training data at all
A single dataset used for all three purposes
Training and test sets only, tuned on test
Separate training, validation, and test sets

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Tuning on validation data preserves the test set for an unbiased final estimate.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Test set only, with no training data at all: A model needs training data.
• A single dataset used for all three purposes: Reusing data inflates performance.
• Training and test sets only, tuned on test: Tuning on test biases the estimate.

Key takeaway: Keep the test set untouched until the end.

stem: A numeric feature has extreme outliers from sensor errors that distort a linear model. Which TWO approaches help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Duplicate outlier rows to balance them
Convert the feature to random categories
Cap or clip values at reasonable percentiles
Multiply the feature by a large constant
Remove records confirmed as sensor errors

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clipping limits extreme values, and removing known errors cleans the data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Duplicate outlier rows to balance them: Duplicating outliers worsens distortion.
• Convert the feature to random categories: Random categories destroy meaning.
• Multiply the feature by a large constant: Scaling does not reduce outlier influence.

Key takeaway: Clip or remove erroneous outliers.

stem: A team must join data from Redshift, S3, and a DynamoDB export to build a training set with SQL, without moving all data first. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon SQS with long polling
Amazon Athena federated queries
AWS Direct Connect links
Amazon Polly speech synthesis

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Athena federated queries join data across sources with SQL.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon SQS with long polling: SQS queues messages.
• AWS Direct Connect links: Direct Connect is networking.
• Amazon Polly speech synthesis: Polly synthesizes speech.

Key takeaway: Query across data sources with Athena federation.

stem: A dataset has a feature 'account_closed_date' that is only filled in after customers churn. A churn model trained with it has nearly perfect validation accuracy. What is the issue?

choices.text: Overfitting caused by too many hyperparameters
Class imbalance caused by the date format used
Target leakage from a feature not available at prediction time
Underfitting caused by too few training epochs and a small model

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Features that encode the outcome and are unavailable at prediction time leak the target.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Overfitting caused by too many hyperparameters: The root cause is leakage, not hyperparameters.
• Class imbalance caused by the date format used: The date format does not create imbalance.
• Underfitting caused by too few training…: Near-perfect accuracy is not underfitting.

Key takeaway: Remove features unavailable at prediction time.

stem: A team wants reusable, code-free data cleaning recipes for tabular data with profiling, run on a schedule. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Kinesis
AWS Glue DataBrew
AWS CodeBuild
Amazon Lex

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DataBrew provides visual recipes, profiling, and scheduled jobs for data preparation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Kinesis: Kinesis streams data.
• AWS CodeBuild: CodeBuild builds code.
• Amazon Lex: Lex builds chatbots.

Key takeaway: Code-free scheduled data prep → DataBrew.

stem: Labels for an image dataset come from several annotators who sometimes disagree. Which practice improves label quality?

choices.text: Let the model assign labels to its own training data
Remove every image that any annotator found hard to label
Use only the first annotation for each item and ignore all of the later ones from other annotators
Collect multiple annotations per item and consolidate them, auditing disagreements

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Consolidating multiple annotations and auditing disagreements improves label accuracy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Let the model assign labels to its own…: Self-labeling reinforces errors.
• Remove every image that any annotator found…: Removing hard items biases data.
• Use only the first annotation for each item…: Single annotations carry individual errors.

Key takeaway: Consolidate multiple annotations.

stem: Which storage option is most cost-effective for keeping large raw training datasets that are read occasionally?

choices.text: EC2 instance store disks
Amazon ElastiCache nodes
Amazon EBS io2 volumes
Amazon S3 with lifecycle rules

explanation:
Why this is correct:
S3 is durable and low cost, and lifecycle rules move rarely used data to cheaper tiers.

Why the other options are wrong:
• EC2 instance store disks: Instance store is ephemeral.
• Amazon ElastiCache nodes: ElastiCache is expensive memory.
• Amazon EBS io2 volumes: io2 is expensive.

Key takeaway: Store raw data in S3 with lifecycle rules.

stem: A model uses a date feature. Which transformation typically helps a tree model capture weekly and monthly patterns?

choices.text: One-hot encode every unique timestamp value
Extract components such as day of week and month
Drop the date because trees cannot use dates
Convert the date into one very large integer only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Extracting calendar components exposes periodic patterns.

Why the other options are wrong:
• One-hot encode every unique timestamp value: Unique timestamps create useless sparse columns.
• Drop the date because trees cannot use dates: Dates can be useful after transformation.
• Convert the date into one very large integer…: A single integer hides periodicity.

Key takeaway: Engineer calendar features from dates.

stem: Which TWO checks help ensure training data is representative of production data? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Verify that file names follow a consistent naming pattern
Confirm that the dataset is stored as CSV rather than Parquet
Check that important segments appear in adequate proportions
Ensure that the data was collected on weekdays only
Compare feature distributions between training and recent production data

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Distribution comparisons and segment coverage checks reveal mismatches between training and production.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Verify that file names follow a consistent…: File naming is irrelevant.
• Confirm that the dataset is stored as CSV…: File format does not affect representativeness.
• Ensure that the data was collected on…: Weekday-only data may be unrepresentative.

Key takeaway: Check distributions and segment coverage.

stem: A team needs to process 50 TB of raw data with Spark before training, and wants a managed, serverless option. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Lambda with a 15-minute timeout
A single EC2 instance running pandas
Amazon Lightsail with a large plan
EMR Serverless or AWS Glue Spark jobs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EMR Serverless and Glue run Spark at scale without managing clusters.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Lambda with a 15-minute timeout: Lambda limits make this impractical.
• A single EC2 instance running pandas: One instance with pandas cannot handle 50 TB well.
• Amazon Lightsail with a large plan: Lightsail is not for big data processing.

Key takeaway: Large-scale serverless Spark → EMR Serverless or Glue.

stem: Two features are highly correlated and cause unstable coefficients in a linear model. Which approach helps?

choices.text: Convert both features into text strings
Increase the learning rate to converge faster
Remove one feature, combine them, or apply regularization
Duplicate both features to strengthen the signal

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Reducing collinearity or regularizing stabilizes linear coefficients.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Convert both features into text strings: Text conversion is not appropriate.
• Increase the learning rate to converge faster: Learning rate does not fix collinearity.
• Duplicate both features to strengthen the signal: Duplication worsens collinearity.

Key takeaway: Address multicollinearity in linear models.

stem: A dataset's labels were generated by a rule-based system that is known to be wrong 10% of the time. Which approach improves the resulting model?

choices.text: Train longer so the model memorizes the noisy labels exactly
Audit and relabel a sample to measure and correct label noise
Add more features so the model can explain the label errors
Report accuracy only on the noisy labels as ground truth

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Measuring and reducing label noise improves both training and evaluation.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Train longer so the model memorizes the…: Memorizing noise hurts generalization.
• Add more features so the model can explain…: Features cannot fix wrong labels.
• Report accuracy only on the noisy labels as…: Noisy evaluation is misleading.

Key takeaway: Measure and reduce label noise.

stem: A team wants to version datasets used for each training run so results are reproducible. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Keep each run's training data only in the data scientist's notebook memory until the session ends
Store immutable dataset snapshots in S3 with versioning and record their URIs with each run
Overwrite the same S3 key with new data before every training run
Delete old datasets after training to save storage costs immediately

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Immutable, versioned datasets tracked with each run enable reproducibility.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Keep each run's training data only in the…: Notebook memory is not durable.
• Overwrite the same S3 key with new data…: Overwriting loses history.
• Delete old datasets after training to save…: Deleting data prevents reproduction.

Key takeaway: Version datasets for reproducibility.

stem: Which TWO practices prevent data leakage during feature engineering? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Include post-outcome features in training
Normalize using statistics from the test set
Compute target statistics on the full dataset
Use pipelines that apply the same fitted steps at inference
Fit transformations on training folds only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Fitting on training data only and applying fitted steps consistently prevent leakage.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Include post-outcome features in training: Post-outcome features leak the target.
• Normalize using statistics from the test set: Test statistics leak information.
• Compute target statistics on the full dataset: Full-data target statistics leak labels.

Key takeaway: Fit on training data; apply the same pipeline everywhere.

stem: A company wants to predict customer churn from tabular data with numeric and categorical features, and needs strong accuracy quickly. Which built-in algorithm is a good first choice?

choices.text: DeepAR
BlazingText
XGBoost
Object Detection

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Gradient-boosted trees such as XGBoost perform strongly on tabular classification.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DeepAR: DeepAR forecasts time series.
• BlazingText: BlazingText handles text embeddings and classification.
• Object Detection: Object Detection handles images.

Key takeaway: Tabular classification → XGBoost as a strong baseline.

stem: A retailer must forecast demand for thousands of related products, using patterns shared across products. Which algorithm fits?

choices.text: Linear Learner regression per product only
K-means clustering
Random Cut Forest
DeepAR forecasting

explanation:
Why this is correct:
DeepAR trains a single model across many related time series, learning shared patterns.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Linear Learner regression per product only: Separate linear models miss shared patterns.
• K-means clustering: K-means clusters data.
• Random Cut Forest: RCF detects anomalies.

Key takeaway: Many related time series → DeepAR.

stem: A company wants to detect unusual spikes in server metrics without labeled anomaly data. Which algorithm fits?

choices.text: XGBoost classifier
Random Cut Forest
Factorization Machines
Linear Learner

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Random Cut Forest detects anomalies in unlabeled data.

Why the other options are wrong:
• XGBoost classifier: XGBoost classification needs labels.
• Factorization Machines: Factorization Machines suit sparse recommendation data.
• Linear Learner: Linear Learner needs labels for supervised tasks.

Key takeaway: Unsupervised anomaly detection → Random Cut Forest.

stem: A recommendation dataset has user-item interactions that are extremely sparse. Which built-in algorithm is designed for this?

choices.text: DeepAR forecasting
Image Classification
Factorization Machines
Semantic Segmentation

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Factorization Machines model interactions in high-dimensional sparse data such as recommendations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• DeepAR forecasting: DeepAR forecasts time series.
• Image Classification: Image Classification is for images.
• Semantic Segmentation: Semantic Segmentation labels image pixels.

Key takeaway: Sparse interaction data → Factorization Machines.

stem: A team wants to classify support tickets using a pretrained language model with little labeled data and minimal infrastructure work. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Use K-means clustering and treat clusters as labels
Use Random Cut Forest to detect ticket categories
Train a large transformer from scratch on 500 examples
Fine-tune a pretrained model from SageMaker JumpStart

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Transfer learning from a pretrained model works well with limited labeled data, and JumpStart simplifies it.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Use K-means clustering and treat clusters as…: Clusters are not reliable labels.
• Use Random Cut Forest to detect ticket…: RCF detects anomalies.
• Train a large transformer from scratch on…: Training from scratch needs far more data.

Key takeaway: Little data → fine-tune pretrained models.

stem: A business team without ML expertise wants to build a model from a spreadsheet with no code. Which option fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Neo compiler
SageMaker distributed training
Amazon SageMaker Canvas
Custom training containers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Canvas lets business users build ML models visually without code.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SageMaker Neo compiler: Neo compiles models for devices.
• SageMaker distributed training: Distributed training requires ML engineering.
• Custom training containers: Custom containers require code.

Key takeaway: No-code ML → SageMaker Canvas.

stem: Training accuracy is 99%, but validation accuracy is 70%. Which TWO actions help? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Train for many more epochs on the same data
Use early stopping based on validation loss
Remove the validation set from the process
Increase model complexity with more layers
Add regularization such as L2 or dropout

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Regularization and early stopping reduce overfitting.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Train for many more epochs on the same data: More epochs increase overfitting.
• Remove the validation set from the process: Removing validation hides the problem.
• Increase model complexity with more layers: More complexity increases overfitting.

Key takeaway: Fight overfitting with regularization and early stopping.

stem: Both training and validation errors are high. What is the most likely issue and fix?

choices.text: Data leakage; remove features from the validation set only
Underfitting; use a more expressive model or better features
Class imbalance; delete the majority class from the data
Overfitting; add stronger regularization and more dropout

explanation:
Why this is correct:
High training and validation errors indicate underfitting, addressed with capacity or better features.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data leakage; remove features from the…: Leakage usually inflates validation scores.
• Class imbalance; delete the majority class…: Deleting data is not a fix for underfitting.
• Overfitting; add stronger regularization and…: Regularization worsens underfitting.

Key takeaway: High train and validation error → underfitting.

stem: A team wants to find good hyperparameters efficiently with fewer training jobs than grid search. Which tuning strategy fits?

choices.text: Manually changing one value per week based on intuition
Exhaustive grid search over every possible combination
Using the same default hyperparameters for every problem
Bayesian optimization in SageMaker Automatic Model Tuning

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bayesian optimization uses previous results to choose promising hyperparameters, needing fewer jobs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Manually changing one value per week based…: Manual weekly changes are slow.
• Exhaustive grid search over every possible…: Grid search is expensive.
• Using the same default hyperparameters for…: Defaults may be poor.

Key takeaway: Efficient tuning → Bayesian optimization.

stem: Many tuning jobs clearly perform poorly after a few epochs, wasting compute. Which feature helps?

choices.text: Running all jobs to completion before comparing results
Increasing the maximum number of concurrent training jobs in the tuning job
Early stopping of training jobs in automatic model tuning (or Hyperband)
Using larger instance types for every tuning job

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Early stopping or Hyperband stops unpromising jobs early, saving compute.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Running all jobs to completion before…: Running all jobs to completion wastes compute.
• Increasing the maximum number of concurrent…: More concurrency does not stop waste.
• Using larger instance types for every tuning job: Larger instances increase cost.

Key takeaway: Stop bad tuning jobs early.

stem: A training job on Spot Instances may be interrupted. Which setting prevents losing progress?

choices.text: Checkpointing to S3 with managed spot training
Increasing the number of training epochs per job
Using a smaller batch size for training
Disabling data shuffling during training

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Checkpoints let interrupted Spot training resume from the last saved state.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Increasing the number of training epochs per job: More epochs do not save progress.
• Using a smaller batch size for training: Batch size does not preserve progress.
• Disabling data shuffling during training: Shuffling is unrelated.

Key takeaway: Managed spot training needs checkpointing.

stem: A deep learning model is too large to fit in a single GPU's memory. Which training approach fits?

choices.text: Reducing the dataset to fit in memory
Model parallelism across multiple GPUs
Training on CPU instances with more RAM
Data parallelism with the full model per GPU

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model parallelism splits the model across devices when it does not fit on one.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Reducing the dataset to fit in memory: Dataset size does not fix model size.
• Training on CPU instances with more RAM: CPU training is too slow for large models.
• Data parallelism with the full model per GPU: Data parallelism still needs the full model on each GPU.

Key takeaway: Model too large for one GPU → model parallelism.

stem: A model fits on one GPU, but training on a huge dataset takes too long. Which approach speeds training?

choices.text: Model parallelism splitting layers across devices
Training on one GPU with a smaller learning rate
Distributed data parallel training across multiple GPUs
Using a single CPU instance with more cores

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data parallelism splits data across GPUs, each with a model copy, speeding training.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Model parallelism splitting layers across…: Model parallelism is for models that do not fit.
• Training on one GPU with a smaller learning rate: Smaller learning rates slow convergence.
• Using a single CPU instance with more cores: CPUs are slower for deep learning.

Key takeaway: Large data, model fits → data parallelism.

stem: A neural network's training loss stops improving, and the team suspects vanishing gradients. Which tool can detect this during training?

choices.text: SageMaker Model Monitor data quality
SageMaker Ground Truth labeling jobs
SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias
SageMaker Debugger with built-in rules

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Debugger captures tensors and has rules for issues such as vanishing gradients.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SageMaker Model Monitor data quality: Model Monitor watches deployed models.
• SageMaker Ground Truth labeling jobs: Ground Truth labels data.
• SageMaker Clarify pre-training bias: Clarify checks bias.

Key takeaway: Diagnose training issues with Debugger.

stem: A medical screening model must miss as few positive cases as possible. Which metric should be prioritized?

choices.text: Overall accuracy
Training loss
Recall (sensitivity)
Precision only

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Recall measures the share of actual positives correctly identified, minimizing missed cases.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Overall accuracy: Accuracy can hide missed positives.
• Training loss: Training loss is not a business metric.
• Precision only: Precision focuses on false positives.

Key takeaway: Minimize missed positives → recall.

stem: A spam filter must rarely flag legitimate emails as spam. Which metric matters most?

choices.text: Recall for the spam class
Precision for the spam class
Mean absolute error
R-squared value

explanation:
Why this is correct:
High precision means few legitimate emails are wrongly flagged.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Recall for the spam class: Recall focuses on catching all spam.
• Mean absolute error: MAE is for regression.
• R-squared value: R-squared is for regression.

Key takeaway: Avoid false positives → precision.

stem: A team needs a threshold-independent metric to compare binary classifiers on imbalanced data. Which TWO metrics fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Accuracy at a 0.5 threshold only
Number of training epochs used
Root mean squared error only
Area under the precision-recall curve
Area under the ROC curve (AUC)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
ROC AUC and PR AUC summarize performance across thresholds; PR AUC is especially informative for imbalance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Accuracy at a 0.5 threshold only: Accuracy at one threshold depends on the threshold and hides imbalance.
• Number of training epochs used: Epochs are not a metric.
• Root mean squared error only: RMSE is for regression.

Key takeaway: Compare classifiers across thresholds with AUC metrics.

stem: Stakeholders want to understand which features most influenced individual predictions of a credit model. Which tool fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Clarify SHAP-based explanations
SageMaker Data Wrangler flows
SageMaker Inference Recommender
SageMaker Neo model compilation jobs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Clarify computes SHAP values to explain feature contributions for predictions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SageMaker Data Wrangler flows: Data Wrangler prepares data.
• SageMaker Inference Recommender: Inference Recommender sizes endpoints.
• SageMaker Neo model compilation jobs: Neo optimizes models.

Key takeaway: Explain predictions with Clarify SHAP.

stem: A regression model predicting house prices is evaluated. Which metric expresses average error in the same units as the target?

choices.text: Root mean squared error (RMSE)
F1 score for each price band
Precision at the top 10
Area under the ROC curve

explanation:
Why this is correct:
RMSE is in the same units as the target, representing typical error size.

Why the other options are wrong:
• F1 score for each price band: F1 is for classification.
• Precision at the top 10: Precision at k is for ranking.
• Area under the ROC curve: AUC is for classification.

Key takeaway: Regression error in target units → RMSE or MAE.

stem: A team wants to compare several trained model versions and approve the best one for deployment with lineage tracking. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Email threads where data scientists vote on the model to deploy
Model artifacts stored in the same S3 key and overwritten each time
SageMaker Model Registry with model package groups and approval status
A spreadsheet listing S3 paths for each model artifact file

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model Registry versions models, stores metrics and lineage, and tracks approval.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Email threads where data scientists vote on…: Emails are not governed records.
• Model artifacts stored in the same S3 key…: Overwriting loses history.
• A spreadsheet listing S3 paths for each…: Spreadsheets lack lineage and control.

Key takeaway: Version and approve models with Model Registry.

stem: A team wants to quickly generate baseline models and leaderboards from tabular data, with the option to inspect generated notebooks. Which feature fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Edge Manager
SageMaker Feature Store
SageMaker Ground Truth
SageMaker Autopilot (AutoML)

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Autopilot automatically builds and ranks candidate models and provides notebooks.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SageMaker Edge Manager: Edge Manager manages edge models.
• SageMaker Feature Store: Feature Store stores features.
• SageMaker Ground Truth: Ground Truth labels data.

Key takeaway: Quick AutoML baselines → Autopilot.

stem: A team needs to adapt a foundation model to a company-specific writing style with a few thousand labeled examples, without managing infrastructure. Which option fits?

choices.text: Store the examples in a vector database and skip fine-tuning
Fine-tune the model in Amazon Bedrock with a customization job
Train a new foundation model from scratch on EC2 instances
Use K-means on the examples and generate text from clusters

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bedrock customization jobs fine-tune supported models on labeled data without infrastructure management.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Store the examples in a vector database and…: Retrieval does not teach writing style reliably.
• Train a new foundation model from scratch on…: Training from scratch is costly and unnecessary.
• Use K-means on the examples and generate…: K-means does not generate text.

Key takeaway: Managed foundation model fine-tuning → Bedrock customization.

stem: A model's training loss oscillates wildly and does not converge. Which hyperparameter change is most likely to help?

choices.text: Increase the learning rate
Remove all regularization
Increase number of classes
Reduce the learning rate

explanation:
Why this is correct:
A learning rate that is too high causes oscillation; lowering it stabilizes training.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Increase the learning rate: Higher rates worsen oscillation.
• Remove all regularization: Regularization is not the cause.
• Increase number of classes: Class count is fixed by the problem.

Key takeaway: Oscillating loss → lower the learning rate.

stem: Which TWO techniques reduce training time and cost for large deep learning jobs? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Mixed-precision training on supported GPUs
Disabling all data loaders' parallelism
Training every model from random weights
Using the largest instance for small jobs
Managed spot training with checkpoints

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Mixed precision speeds computation, and Spot pricing reduces cost with checkpoints protecting progress.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disabling all data loaders' parallelism: Serial data loading slows training.
• Training every model from random weights: Transfer learning is usually cheaper.
• Using the largest instance for small jobs: Oversized instances waste money.

Key takeaway: Cut training cost with mixed precision and Spot.

stem: A binary classifier's confusion matrix shows many false negatives. What does this mean?

choices.text: The dataset contains no negative examples at all
Many actual negatives were predicted as positive
Many actual positives were predicted as negative
The model predicts positives perfectly in all cases

explanation:
Why this is correct:
False negatives are positive cases incorrectly predicted as negative.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The dataset contains no negative examples at all: Negatives exist in the matrix.
• Many actual negatives were predicted as positive: That describes false positives.
• The model predicts positives perfectly in…: False negatives mean positives were missed.

Key takeaway: False negative = missed positive.

stem: A model performs well overall but poorly for one customer segment. What should the team do before deployment?

choices.text: Deploy anyway because the overall metric meets the target threshold
Evaluate metrics per segment and address data or model gaps for that segment
Increase the classification threshold only for that segment's users
Remove that segment's customers from the evaluation set so the overall scores go up

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Segment-level evaluation reveals disparities that should be fixed with better data or modeling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deploy anyway because the overall metric…: Overall metrics hide segment failures.
• Increase the classification threshold only…: Arbitrary threshold changes may cause unfairness without fixing the model.
• Remove that segment's customers from the…: Removing data hides problems.

Key takeaway: Evaluate performance per segment.

stem: A company needs image classification for 20 product categories with a few hundred images each and minimal ML expertise. Which option fits?

choices.text: Amazon Comprehend custom classes
Amazon Rekognition Custom Labels
Amazon Textract queries
Amazon Forecast predictors

explanation:

Rekognition Custom Labels trains image classifiers from a small labeled dataset with minimal ML expertise.

stem: A team wants to track experiments, parameters, and metrics across many training runs for comparison. Which option fits?

choices.text: SageMaker managed MLflow experiment tracking
S3 server access logs for the model bucket
CloudTrail management events for each job
AWS Config configuration recorder history

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Managed MLflow tracks runs, parameters, and metrics for comparison.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 server access logs for the model bucket: Access logs record S3 requests.
• CloudTrail management events for each job: CloudTrail records API calls.
• AWS Config configuration recorder history: Config records configurations.

Key takeaway: Track experiments with managed MLflow.

stem: A team must choose a classification threshold that balances business costs of false positives and false negatives. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Pick the threshold that produces the fewest positive predictions
Always use a threshold of 0.5 because it is the standard default value
Choose the threshold that maximizes accuracy regardless of costs
Compute expected cost across thresholds and pick the minimum-cost threshold

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Cost-based threshold selection aligns the model's decisions with business impact.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Pick the threshold that produces the fewest…: Fewest positives may miss many true cases.
• Always use a threshold of 0.5 because it is…: 0.5 ignores costs.
• Choose the threshold that maximizes accuracy…: Accuracy ignores asymmetric costs.

Key takeaway: Choose thresholds by business cost.

stem: A team can use a simple interpretable model with slightly lower accuracy or a complex model with higher accuracy. Regulators require explanations of individual decisions. Which choice fits?

choices.text: Choose the model with the most parameters, because it will always be the more accurate choice
Avoid ML entirely because no model can ever be explained
Prefer the interpretable model, or use the complex model only with robust explanation tooling
Choose the complex model and provide no explanations to regulators

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Regulatory explainability needs may favor interpretable models or require strong explanation tools.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Choose the model with the most parameters,…: Parameter count is not a requirement.
• Avoid ML entirely because no model can ever…: Many models can be explained.
• Choose the complex model and provide no…: Ignoring requirements is noncompliant.

Key takeaway: Balance accuracy with explainability requirements.

stem: A model must return predictions within 100 ms for an interactive web application with steady traffic. Which deployment option fits?

choices.text: A SageMaker real-time endpoint
SageMaker batch transform job
A nightly scheduled processing job
SageMaker asynchronous endpoint

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Real-time endpoints serve low-latency, synchronous predictions.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SageMaker batch transform job: Batch transform is offline.
• A nightly scheduled processing job: Nightly jobs are offline.
• SageMaker asynchronous endpoint: Async endpoints queue requests.

Key takeaway: Low-latency online predictions → real-time endpoints.

stem: A model receives a few requests per hour with long idle periods, and cold-start latency of a few seconds is acceptable. Which option minimizes cost?

choices.text: A batch transform job run every minute
A multi-model endpoint kept always on
A real-time endpoint on GPU instances
SageMaker Serverless Inference

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Serverless Inference scales to zero when idle and charges per use.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A batch transform job run every minute: Per-minute batch jobs are inefficient.
• A multi-model endpoint kept always on: Always-on endpoints cost money when idle.
• A real-time endpoint on GPU instances: Always-on GPUs cost money when idle.

Key takeaway: Intermittent traffic with tolerable cold starts → Serverless Inference.

stem: Predictions are needed for 50 million records once a week, and results can be written to S3. Which option fits?

choices.text: An EC2 instance with a web server
SageMaker real-time endpoint
SageMaker batch transform
SageMaker Serverless Inference

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Batch transform processes large datasets offline without a persistent endpoint.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An EC2 instance with a web server: A web server is unnecessary.
• SageMaker real-time endpoint: Real-time endpoints are for online requests.
• SageMaker Serverless Inference: Serverless suits sporadic online traffic.

Key takeaway: Large offline scoring → batch transform.

stem: Requests include 500 MB video files and take several minutes to process. Clients can poll for results. Which option fits?

choices.text: AWS Lambda synchronous invocation
SageMaker asynchronous inference
SageMaker Serverless Inference
SageMaker real-time inference

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Async inference supports large payloads and long processing, with results written to S3.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Lambda synchronous invocation: Lambda has payload and time limits.
• SageMaker Serverless Inference: Serverless has payload and duration limits.
• SageMaker real-time inference: Real-time has payload and timeout limits.

Key takeaway: Large payloads and long processing → async inference.

stem: A company hosts 500 small per-customer models with infrequent traffic each. Which option reduces hosting cost?

choices.text: A multi-model endpoint loading models on demand
A batch transform job for each individual request
A separate EC2 instance for each customer model
A separate real-time endpoint for each model

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Multi-model endpoints share instances and load models from S3 as needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A batch transform job for each individual…: Batch jobs per request are slow.
• A separate EC2 instance for each customer model: 500 instances cost far more.
• A separate real-time endpoint for each model: 500 endpoints cost far more.

Key takeaway: Many small models → multi-model endpoints.

stem: A team needs to choose the most cost-effective instance type for a model endpoint that meets latency targets. Which tool fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Clarify bias reports
SageMaker Data Wrangler flows
SageMaker Ground Truth labeling
SageMaker Inference Recommender

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inference Recommender load-tests instance types and recommends configurations meeting latency and cost goals.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SageMaker Clarify bias reports: Clarify reports bias.
• SageMaker Data Wrangler flows: Data Wrangler prepares data.
• SageMaker Ground Truth labeling: Ground Truth labels data.

Key takeaway: Right-size endpoints with Inference Recommender.

stem: A model must run on edge devices with limited compute. Which tool optimizes it for the target hardware?

choices.text: SageMaker Canvas
SageMaker Neo
SageMaker Clarify
SageMaker Autopilot

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Neo compiles models for specific hardware to improve performance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SageMaker Canvas: Canvas is no-code ML.
• SageMaker Clarify: Clarify explains and checks bias.
• SageMaker Autopilot: Autopilot builds models.

Key takeaway: Optimize models for edge hardware with Neo.

stem: Before promoting a new model, a team wants to send a copy of production traffic to it and compare its responses without affecting users. Which feature fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Canvas quick model builds
SageMaker batch transform on old data
SageMaker shadow testing (shadow variants)
SageMaker Feature Store offline queries

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Shadow tests mirror production requests to a shadow variant and compare results without serving its responses.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SageMaker Canvas quick model builds: Canvas does not test endpoints.
• SageMaker batch transform on old data: Old data is not live traffic.
• SageMaker Feature Store offline queries: Feature Store queries features.

Key takeaway: Validate with mirrored live traffic → shadow testing.

stem: A real-time endpoint's traffic varies during the day. Which configuration adjusts instance count automatically?

choices.text: A fixed instance count set to the daily peak
Manual updates of the endpoint every hour
Endpoint auto scaling with target tracking on InvocationsPerInstance
Creating a brand new endpoint by hand for each traffic spike

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Auto scaling adjusts instances based on invocations per instance.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A fixed instance count set to the daily peak: A fixed peak count wastes money.
• Manual updates of the endpoint every hour: Manual updates are slow.
• Creating a brand new endpoint by hand for…: New endpoints per spike are impractical.

Key takeaway: Scale endpoints on invocations per instance.

stem: A team must deploy endpoints consistently across dev, staging, and prod accounts. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Copy the model artifact by email to each account's administrator, who then deploys it by hand
Create endpoints manually in the console in each account for each release
Use one shared endpoint in dev for all environments, including production
Define endpoints and configurations in CloudFormation or CDK and deploy through a pipeline

explanation:
Why this is correct:
IaC with pipelines deploys consistent endpoint configurations across accounts.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Copy the model artifact by email to each…: Email is not a deployment method.
• Create endpoints manually in the console in…: Manual creation drifts.
• Use one shared endpoint in dev for all…: Sharing a dev endpoint for production is risky.

Key takeaway: Deploy ML infrastructure as code.

stem: A team wants to bring a custom inference container with its own dependencies to SageMaker. Where must the image be stored?

choices.text: Amazon ECR
AWS CodeCommit
Amazon EFS only
Amazon S3 Glacier

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker pulls custom container images from Amazon ECR.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS CodeCommit: CodeCommit stores source code.
• Amazon EFS only: EFS is a file system, not an image registry.
• Amazon S3 Glacier: Glacier is archival storage.

Key takeaway: Custom containers are stored in ECR.

stem: An endpoint needs different compute resources per model while sharing instances, with independent scaling per model. Which feature fits?

choices.text: A single container that loads all of the models
Inference components on a SageMaker endpoint
A Lambda function per model with no GPU
Separate batch transform jobs per model

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inference components let multiple models share an endpoint with per-model resource allocation and scaling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A single container that loads all of the models: A single container cannot allocate resources per model.
• A Lambda function per model with no GPU: Lambda lacks GPUs.
• Separate batch transform jobs per model: Batch jobs are offline.

Key takeaway: Share endpoints with per-model resources → inference components.

stem: A preprocessing step and a model must run in sequence for each request at one endpoint. Which feature fits?

choices.text: A multi-model endpoint with one model
A serial inference pipeline of containers
Two separate endpoints called by users
Batch transform with a manual step

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Inference pipelines chain containers so each request flows through preprocessing and the model.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A multi-model endpoint with one model: Multi-model endpoints host independent models.
• Two separate endpoints called by users: Separate endpoints push orchestration to clients.
• Batch transform with a manual step: Batch transform is offline.

Key takeaway: Chain preprocessing and model → inference pipeline.

stem: A team wants a repeatable workflow of processing, training, evaluation, conditional registration, and deployment. Which service fits?

choices.text: AWS Batch arrays
Amazon SQS queues
SageMaker Pipelines
Amazon SNS topics

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Pipelines orchestrates ML steps with conditions, lineage, and integration with Model Registry.

Why the other options are wrong:
• AWS Batch arrays: Batch array jobs are not ML-aware pipelines.
• Amazon SQS queues: Queues do not orchestrate ML workflows.
• Amazon SNS topics: SNS publishes messages.

Key takeaway: Orchestrate ML workflows with SageMaker Pipelines.

stem: A pipeline should register a model only if its evaluation AUC is at least 0.85. Which step type implements this?

choices.text: A condition step comparing the evaluation metric
A callback step that always waits for a human reviewer
A fail step placed before training runs
A processing step with no outputs at all

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Condition steps branch based on values such as evaluation metrics.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A callback step that always waits for a…: Callbacks wait for external signals.
• A fail step placed before training runs: A fail step stops the pipeline.
• A processing step with no outputs at all: A processing step alone does not branch.

Key takeaway: Gate registration with condition steps.

stem: When a model version is approved in Model Registry, deployment to staging should start automatically. Which design fits?

choices.text: A data scientist emailing the operations team to deploy the approved model
A cron job that redeploys the newest model version every hour regardless
Deploying every registered model version directly to production endpoints
EventBridge rule on the approval status change triggering a deployment pipeline

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Registry state changes emit events that can trigger CI/CD deployments.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A data scientist emailing the operations…: Email is manual.
• A cron job that redeploys the newest model…: Blind redeploys ignore approval.
• Deploying every registered model version…: Deploying unapproved models is risky.

Key takeaway: Trigger deployments from registry approvals.

stem: A team wants separate CI/CD for model building and model deployment with templates provided by SageMaker. Which feature fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Canvas quick builds
SageMaker Projects MLOps templates
SageMaker Ground Truth jobs
SageMaker Studio Lab notebooks

explanation:
Why this is correct:
SageMaker Projects provide MLOps templates with build and deploy pipelines.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SageMaker Canvas quick builds: Canvas is no-code modeling.
• SageMaker Ground Truth jobs: Ground Truth labels data.
• SageMaker Studio Lab notebooks: Studio Lab is a free notebook environment.

Key takeaway: MLOps templates → SageMaker Projects.

stem: A data engineering team already uses Apache Airflow and wants to orchestrate ML training alongside ETL jobs. Which service fits?

choices.text: Amazon Lightsail container service
Amazon Simple Notification Service topics
AWS Elemental MediaConvert jobs
Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow

explanation:
Why this is correct:
MWAA runs managed Airflow, which can orchestrate ETL and SageMaker jobs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Lightsail container service: Lightsail containers are not orchestration.
• Amazon Simple Notification Service topics: SNS publishes messages.
• AWS Elemental MediaConvert jobs: MediaConvert processes video.

Key takeaway: Airflow-based orchestration → MWAA.

stem: A team wants to update a production endpoint with a new model version safely, shifting traffic gradually and rolling back on alarms. Which feature fits?

choices.text: Updating the endpoint all at once during peak business hours
Asking users to switch to a new endpoint name manually
Deployment guardrails with canary or linear traffic shifting
Deleting the endpoint and creating a new one with the new model

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Deployment guardrails shift traffic gradually and roll back automatically based on alarms.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Updating the endpoint all at once during…: All-at-once updates expose all users.
• Asking users to switch to a new endpoint…: Manual switching is error-prone.
• Deleting the endpoint and creating a new one…: Deleting the endpoint causes downtime.

Key takeaway: Safe endpoint updates with deployment guardrails.

stem: Which TWO actions reduce the time for SageMaker endpoint instances to become ready during scale-out? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Use a scaling policy with a suitable cooldown and target
Disable health checks on the endpoint entirely
Store the model artifact in S3 Glacier Deep Archive
Package every unused dependency into the container
Use smaller model artifacts and optimized containers

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Smaller artifacts and optimized containers load faster, and tuned scaling reacts earlier.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Disable health checks on the endpoint entirely: Health checks cannot simply be disabled and are needed.
• Store the model artifact in S3 Glacier Deep…: Deep Archive retrieval takes hours.
• Package every unused dependency into the…: Unused dependencies slow startup.

Key takeaway: Speed scale-out with lean artifacts and tuned scaling.

stem: A lightweight scikit-learn model with low traffic must be served at the lowest operational effort. Which TWO options are reasonable? (Select TWO)

choices.text: SageMaker Serverless Inference
A large EMR cluster kept running
An EKS cluster with GPU node groups
A dedicated GPU real-time endpoint
AWS Lambda with the model packaged in a container image

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Serverless options suit small models with low traffic and minimal operations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A large EMR cluster kept running: EMR is for big data.
• An EKS cluster with GPU node groups: EKS with GPUs adds heavy operations.
• A dedicated GPU real-time endpoint: GPUs are unnecessary and costly.

Key takeaway: Small low-traffic models → serverless serving.

stem: A team wants to deploy JumpStart foundation models to endpoints with a few lines of Python. Which tool fits?

choices.text: The Route 53 console
The SageMaker Python SDK
The IAM credential report
The AWS Billing console

explanation:
Why this is correct:
The SageMaker Python SDK deploys JumpStart models to endpoints programmatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The Route 53 console: Route 53 is DNS.
• The IAM credential report: The credential report lists IAM credentials.
• The AWS Billing console: Billing is unrelated.

Key takeaway: Programmatic deployment → SageMaker Python SDK.

stem: A training pipeline should run automatically when new labeled data lands in S3. Which design fits?

choices.text: A pipeline scheduled once a year regardless of new data arrival
A notebook left running forever that polls the bucket every second
An EventBridge rule on S3 object events starting the SageMaker pipeline
A data scientist checking the bucket each morning and starting training

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Event-driven triggers start pipelines when new data arrives.

Why the other options are wrong:
• A pipeline scheduled once a year regardless…: Yearly runs ignore new data.
• A notebook left running forever that polls…: Always-running notebooks waste resources.
• A data scientist checking the bucket each…: Manual checks are slow.

Key takeaway: Trigger retraining on data arrival.

stem: A pipeline step fails intermittently due to transient errors. Which feature helps without code changes?

choices.text: Running the pipeline only once per month
Removing the failing step from the pipeline
A larger instance for all other steps
Retry policies on the pipeline step

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Step retry policies automatically retry transient failures.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Running the pipeline only once per month: Running less often does not fix failures.
• Removing the failing step from the pipeline: Removing steps breaks the workflow.
• A larger instance for all other steps: Larger instances do not fix transient failures.

Key takeaway: Handle transient failures with retry policies.

stem: A generative model on a SageMaker endpoint must stream tokens back to users as they are generated. Which capability fits?

choices.text: Serverless inference with long polling
Batch transform writing to S3 each hour
Asynchronous inference with results written to S3 only
Response streaming with InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Response streaming returns partial outputs as they are produced.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Serverless inference with long polling: Serverless does not provide token streaming by polling.
• Batch transform writing to S3 each hour: Batch transform is offline.
• Asynchronous inference with results written…: Async writes results when complete.

Key takeaway: Stream model outputs with response streaming.

stem: Which TWO practices make ML deployments reproducible? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Overwrite model artifacts in the same S3 location
Pin container image digests and library versions
Retrain models directly on production endpoints
Install the latest libraries at container startup
Deploy registered model versions with recorded lineage

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Pinned images and versioned, registered models ensure the same artifact and environment are deployed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Overwrite model artifacts in the same S3…: Overwriting loses history.
• Retrain models directly on production endpoints: Retraining in production is uncontrolled.
• Install the latest libraries at container…: Floating versions change behavior.

Key takeaway: Pin environments and deploy registered versions.

stem: A company wants model deployments to require approval from a risk team before production. Which approach fits?

choices.text: A manual approval action in the deployment pipeline tied to Model Registry status
An email sent after deployment so the risk team is informed later
A policy that data scientists deploy directly to production whenever they feel confident enough
Allowing any team to change the endpoint configuration at any time

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Approval gates in the pipeline enforce review before production.

Why the other options are wrong:
• An email sent after deployment so the risk…: Post-deployment emails are too late.
• A policy that data scientists deploy…: Direct deployment bypasses review.
• Allowing any team to change the endpoint…: Uncontrolled changes are risky.

Key takeaway: Gate production deployments with approvals.

stem: A company wants to run inference on Kubernetes because its platform team standardizes on EKS. Which option fits?

choices.text: Use Amazon SQS to host the model and answer requests
Deploy the model to Amazon Lightsail instances without containers
Deploy model servers on Amazon EKS with GPU node groups as needed
Use AWS Glue jobs to serve real-time predictions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
EKS can host containerized model servers with GPU nodes when needed.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Use Amazon SQS to host the model and answer…: SQS is a queue, not a host.
• Deploy the model to Amazon Lightsail…: Lightsail is not a Kubernetes platform.
• Use AWS Glue jobs to serve real-time predictions: Glue is for ETL.

Key takeaway: Kubernetes-standard platforms can serve models on EKS.

stem: A team needs Pipelines steps to reuse results when inputs have not changed, to save time. Which feature fits?

choices.text: S3 lifecycle rules on outputs
Endpoint auto scaling policies
Step caching in SageMaker Pipelines
CloudWatch alarm actions

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Step caching reuses previous outputs when step arguments are unchanged.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 lifecycle rules on outputs: Lifecycle rules manage storage.
• Endpoint auto scaling policies: Auto scaling adjusts endpoints.
• CloudWatch alarm actions: Alarms react to metrics.

Key takeaway: Skip unchanged steps with step caching.

stem: Which service can orchestrate an ML workflow that mixes Lambda, Glue, and SageMaker steps with visual design and error handling?

choices.text: Amazon Inspector
AWS Step Functions
Amazon Route 53
Amazon Kinesis

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Step Functions integrates with many services and provides visual workflows with retries and error handling.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Amazon Inspector: Inspector scans vulnerabilities.
• Amazon Route 53: Route 53 is DNS.
• Amazon Kinesis: Kinesis streams data.

Key takeaway: Cross-service ML orchestration → Step Functions.

stem: A deployed model's input feature distributions may shift over time. The team wants automatic detection compared to a training baseline. Which feature fits?

choices.text: SageMaker Model Monitor data quality monitoring with a baseline
SageMaker Debugger built-in rules attached to the original training job only
SageMaker Ground Truth labeling jobs for new data
SageMaker Neo compilation of the deployed model

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model Monitor compares captured inference data against a baseline and reports violations.

Why the other options are wrong:
• SageMaker Debugger built-in rules attached…: Debugger inspects training, not live data.
• SageMaker Ground Truth labeling jobs for new…: Ground Truth labels data.
• SageMaker Neo compilation of the deployed model: Neo optimizes models.

Key takeaway: Detect data drift with Model Monitor.

stem: A team wants to measure a deployed model's accuracy over time, but labels arrive days after predictions. Which setup fits?

choices.text: Data quality monitoring on inputs only, without any use of labels at all
Retraining the model every hour without evaluating its accuracy first
Comparing the model's latest predictions with its own earlier predictions every hour to check that they stay consistent
Model quality monitoring that merges captured predictions with ground truth labels uploaded later

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Model quality monitoring joins predictions with delayed ground truth to compute metrics such as accuracy.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data quality monitoring on inputs only,…: Input monitoring does not measure accuracy.
• Retraining the model every hour without…: Blind retraining ignores quality.
• Comparing the model's latest predictions…: Self-comparison says nothing about correctness.

Key takeaway: Measure live accuracy by merging delayed labels.

stem: Which prerequisite must be enabled on an endpoint for Model Monitor to analyze requests and responses?

choices.text: Data capture on the endpoint configuration
Managed spot training for the model
Multi-model hosting on the endpoint
Network isolation on the training job

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Data capture records inputs and outputs to S3 for monitoring jobs.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Managed spot training for the model: Spot training is a cost option.
• Multi-model hosting on the endpoint: Multi-model hosting is unrelated.
• Network isolation on the training job: Network isolation is a security setting.

Key takeaway: Enable data capture before monitoring.

stem: A credit model's predictions may become biased against a group as the population changes. Which monitoring type fits?

choices.text: Data capture only, with no scheduled analysis jobs configured on the captured data
CloudWatch CPU utilization alarms on the endpoint
Bias drift monitoring with SageMaker Clarify and Model Monitor
CloudTrail logging of the InvokeEndpoint API calls

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Bias drift monitoring tracks bias metrics on live data over time.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Data capture only, with no scheduled…: Capture without analysis detects nothing.
• CloudWatch CPU utilization alarms on the…: CPU metrics do not show bias.
• CloudTrail logging of the InvokeEndpoint API…: CloudTrail records API calls.

Key takeaway: Monitor fairness over time with bias drift monitoring.

stem: The features that most influence predictions have changed since deployment. Which monitoring type detects this?

choices.text: S3 object versioning on data
Endpoint instance health checks
IAM Access Analyzer findings
Feature attribution drift monitoring

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Feature attribution drift compares feature importance on live data with the baseline.

Why the other options are wrong:
• S3 object versioning on data: Versioning protects objects.
• Endpoint instance health checks: Health checks confirm availability.
• IAM Access Analyzer findings: Access Analyzer reviews permissions.

Key takeaway: Detect changing feature importance with attribution drift monitoring.

stem: When Model Monitor detects data drift above a threshold, the team wants retraining to start automatically. Which design fits?

choices.text: Deleting the endpoint whenever any violation appears in a monitoring report
CloudWatch alarm on monitoring metrics triggering EventBridge to start a SageMaker pipeline
Retraining on a fixed daily schedule regardless of whether drift occurs
A data scientist reading the monitoring reports once each quarter and then retraining the model by hand

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Metric-based alarms and events can trigger retraining pipelines automatically.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Deleting the endpoint whenever any violation…: Deleting endpoints causes outages.
• Retraining on a fixed daily schedule…: Fixed schedules may waste compute or miss urgent drift.
• A data scientist reading the monitoring…: Quarterly manual review is slow.

Key takeaway: Trigger retraining from drift alarms.

stem: Which TWO metrics should be monitored on a real-time endpoint for operational health? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The size of the training data in S3 buckets
Invocation4XXErrors and Invocation5XXErrors
The number of notebooks in SageMaker Studio
The number of labels in Ground Truth jobs
ModelLatency and OverheadLatency

stem: A monitoring job reports drift, but the team is unsure whether it affects business outcomes. What should they check next?

choices.text: The size of the model artifact stored in S3
The date the training container image was built
The number of endpoints in the account and the naming convention they follow
Model quality metrics against ground truth and downstream business KPIs

explanation:
Why this is correct:
Drift matters when it degrades model quality or business results, which must be measured directly.

Why the other options are wrong:
• The size of the model artifact stored in S3: Artifact size is unrelated.
• The date the training container image was built: Image build dates are unrelated.
• The number of endpoints in the account and…: Endpoint counts are unrelated.

Key takeaway: Confirm drift impact with quality metrics and KPIs.

stem: A real-time endpoint runs on a large GPU instance at 5% utilization. Which change reduces cost most directly?

choices.text: Right-size the instance using Inference Recommender or utilization data
Increase the endpoint's data capture percentage
Enable Model Monitor with an hourly schedule
Add a second identical GPU instance to the endpoint for redundancy

Moving to a smaller or cheaper instance that meets latency needs reduces waste.

Why the other options are wrong:
• Increase the endpoint's data capture percentage: Data capture adds storage cost.
• Enable Model Monitor with an hourly schedule: Monitoring adds cost without reducing compute.
• Add a second identical GPU instance to the…: A second instance doubles cost.

Key takeaway: Right-size underutilized endpoints.

stem: A company runs steady SageMaker training and inference workloads for years. Which purchasing option reduces cost?

choices.text: On-demand pricing with alarms
EC2 Reserved Instances only
SageMaker Savings Plans
Dedicated Hosts for SageMaker

explanation:

SageMaker Savings Plans discount steady SageMaker usage.

• EC2 Reserved Instances only: EC2 RIs do not apply to SageMaker instances.
